math/exponents.d0d4ee8f06d2: Question one of twelve. One sheet is eight times ten to the power of minus five meters thick. How thick is a stack of four times ten squared sheets?
math/exponents.b1bae0fd81fa: Given: two files take up three point six times ten to the sixth bytes and nine times ten to the fifth bytes. The transfer rate is one point five times ten to the fifth bytes per second.
math/exponents.c331899ecc37: Now follow a pattern. Going down the list, the exponent drops by one and the value is divided by ten. Keep going past ten to the power of one: next comes ten to the power of zero equals one, then ten to the power of negative one equals one over ten, then ten to the power of negative two equals one over one hundred.
math/exponents.3376397b35c2: Multiply two cubed times two to the power of four. Write out the factors: three twos and four twos. Together that is seven twos, so two cubed times two to the power of four equals two to the power of the quantity three plus four equals two to the power of seven. Same base: add the exponents.
math/exponents.70ffc4b611ef: A folder uses six point two times ten to the sixth bytes. You delete a file of eight times ten to the fifth bytes. How much space do the remaining files use?
math/exponents.0d04c2b3a7c4: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together?
math/exponents.a0b7bf181c2e: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together? Add the two file sizes. Rewrite the second size using the same power of ten. Factor out the shared power of ten. Add the coefficients. The result is in scientific notation.
math/exponents.7ebf94ba4ac2: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together? Add the two file sizes. Rewrite the second size using the same power of ten. Factor out the shared power of ten.
math/exponents.367cc4ee988f: Answer: the combined length is four times ten to the power of minus four meters.
math/exponents.ebddb85c8eaa: Scientific notation tames huge numbers. The Sun is about one hundred fifty million kilometers away. Hop the decimal point left until just one nonzero digit is in front of it: eight hops, so the distance is one point five times ten to the power of eight kilometers.
math/exponents.a27e65bf4b2c: Worked example: the Sun is about one point five times ten to the power of eight kilometers from Earth and the Moon is about three point eight times ten to the power of five kilometers from Earth. About how many Earth-Moon distances fit into one Earth-Sun distance? Divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents: one point five over three point eight, times ten to the power of the quantity eight minus five is about zero point four times ten cubed equals four hundred. About four hundred times!
math/exponents.1b23bdaea007: Question one of three. A calculator returns two point five E minus four for a length in meters. Which length is that?
math/exponents.88b557a46d7d: Equal to ten to the sixth
math/exponents.7d2480b28324: In round one, you share a video with two friends. At every round, each person from the previous round shares it with two more people. If every share reaches a different new viewer, how many new viewers are there in round twenty? A positive whole-number exponent counts copies of the base used as factors.
math/exponents.99f513fa3386: In the Rule lab, set the quotient to m equals n and then m is less than n and discuss a to the zero power and a to the power of negative n.
math/exponents.1b5e7334138f: A folder uses six point two times ten to the sixth bytes. You delete a file of eight times ten to the fifth bytes. How much space do the remaining files use? Subtract the deleted file size.
math/exponents.d03f65d1925a: A camera saves two thousand four hundred images, each using six point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How much storage do they need? Multiply one image’s size by the number of images.
math/exponents.a8495c0f6eb9: A positive integer exponent counts how many copies of the base are multiplied. A three-by-three square has three times three equals three squared equals nine tiles; a three-by-three-by-three cube has three times three times three equals three cubed equals twenty-seven blocks. In three to the power of four, three is the base and four is the exponent.
math/exponents.646cad69d77c: So for any nonzero base: a to the power of zero equals one and a to the power of negative n equals one over a to the power of n. The quotient rule agrees: two cubed over two cubed equals two to the power of the quantity three minus three equals two to the power of zero, and any nonzero number divided by itself is one. Example: two to the power of negative three equals one over two cubed equals one over eight.
math/exponents.67f0aa9cf880: Divide two to the power of six over two squared. Each two on the bottom cancels one two on top. Four twos survive: two to the power of six over two squared equals two to the power of the quantity six minus two equals two to the power of four equals sixteen. Same base: subtract the exponents.
math/exponents.442e699ac704: x to the power of fifteen
math/exponents.de40f750467a: Question one of two. A ten to the power of minus six meter view gets ten times wider. What is its new width?
math/exponents.eb622b08ee55: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together? Add the two file sizes.
math/exponents.6c52aee60d8a: Tiny numbers work the same way in reverse. A human hair is about zero point zero zero zero zero seven meters thick. Hop the point right five places to land after the seven: seven times ten to the power of negative five meters. Hops to the right give a negative exponent.

math/expressions.79640367fc1f: Let a blue bar stand for x and a small yellow square stand for one. Words turn into pictures, and pictures into expressions: “three more than a number” is x plus three; “triple a number” is three x, which means three times x.
math/expressions.e7d75190c4e6: Common mix-up: three times the quantity x plus two is NOT three x plus two! The three multiplies every term inside, so it is three x plus six. And x plus three can't be combined into three x: a bar and a square are not like terms.
math/expressions.64ca4874a89b: Memory hint: “The number outside shakes hands with everyone inside”: a shakes hands with b, then with c, giving a b plus a c.
math/expressions.0aa2ce90e093: Once we know what is in the box, we can evaluate. If x equals four, every bar is really four squares long. Count: four, eight, twelve, then thirteen, fourteen. So three x plus two equals three times four plus two equals fourteen.
math/expressions.fcbf003102e5: Now an area picture. A rectangle three tall and six wide holds three times six equals eighteen squares. Cut it into two pieces, three times four equals twelve and three times two equals six: together still eighteen. So three times the quantity four plus two equals three times four plus three times two.
math/expressions.8cea90daaab8: Now replace the four with an unknown length x. The blue piece becomes three x-bars, area three x; the yellow piece is still six. So three times the quantity x plus two equals three x plus six, whatever x is.
math/expressions.51aab55e4e51: Imagine a box holding some marbles. We don’t know how many, and the number could change: three, seven, twelve … So we give the box a name, a letter such as x. That letter is a variable.
math/expressions.be84948185e2: Factoring runs it backwards. Take the tiles of four x plus eight and arrange them into a rectangle with identical rows. It is four tall and x plus two wide, so four x plus eight equals four times the quantity x plus two.
math/expressions.b9114834844c: Worked example: simplify two times the quantity three x plus one, plus four x. Distribute the two: six x plus two plus four x. Combine like terms: ten x plus two. Check with x equals one: both forms give twelve.
math/expressions.55a177ef3454: Like terms are tiles with the same shape. In two x plus three plus x plus one, slide the bars together and the squares together: three x plus four. A bar and a square can never merge, because x and one are different sizes.

math/factoring.eaa2a68ccd1d: The four pieces fill a square of side a plus b. Both a b rectangles belong in the middle term.
math/factoring.88bad3cb215b: Set the number of unit spaces on each side. Pick a tile and tap a matching space. Tap a placed tile to take it back. The board draws x as two units long.
math/factoring.81fcbaa3f57a: Factor out the shared bracket. Expanding gives six x squared plus thirteen x plus six after combining like terms.
math/factoring.f7603fa24579: The two pieces now form a rectangle with sides a plus b and a minus b.
math/factoring.49afcfb9d516: The ends are squares of two x and five. Check that the middle is minus two times two x times five.
math/factoring.0617cd77b0a3: The coefficients share a factor of three. Both terms contain x, so the greatest common factor is three x.
math/factoring.c36efef5da1b: Factor three x from the first group and two from the second. Now two x plus three is a common factor.
math/factoring.a0d41652433b: Multiply every term in one factor by every term in the other, then combine like terms. The drawing uses x equals two and the absolute values of the coefficients for its lengths. Stripes mark products with negative coefficients.
math/factoring.b775d4747f77: Read the rows as x plus m and x plus n. To factor x squared plus p x plus q this way, the integers m and n must add to p and multiply to q.
math/factoring.2538e77694db: Identify the two squares and their bases: three x and four.

math/fractals.56add850d2a8: Each point is a complex number c, which has two coordinates. Start at zero and keep squaring the result and adding the same c. The values of c whose results stay within some fixed distance of zero forever make up the Mandelbrot set. Colors show how quickly points escape, and dark pixels show points that haven’t escaped within the drawing’s step limit.
math/fractals.a668976fc959: Build a tiny equilateral triangle outward on the middle third of each edge and erase its base. One edge becomes four edges a third as long, so the perimeter multiplies by four over three each round and grows without bound. After the first round, each round adds four ninths as much area as the previous round added, and the total area approaches one point six times the starting area.
math/fractals.b12889f2d39a: The trunk is level one. Each extra level grows two shorter branches from every tip in the previous level. The angle tells how far each new branch turns from the old branch’s direction, and the length ratio compares one new branch with the branch it grew from.

math/fraction-division.7bbd5faa88e9: Why does this work? Measure everything in the same unit, thirds. Three is nine over three and a piece is two over three. How many twos fit in nine? Nine over three, divided by two over three, equals nine divided by two equals four and a half. Same denominator, so just divide the numerators.
math/fraction-division.1f31de6aaf48: What if it does not fit evenly? In three divided by two thirds, four pieces fit and one third is left over. That leftover is half a piece, so the answer is four and a half, not four and a third.
math/fraction-division.b7e1ab0115e0: Common mix-up: Measure the leftover in PIECES, not in wholes. In three divided by two thirds, four pieces fit and one third is left; that one third is half a piece, so the answer is four and a half, not four and a third. And flip only the divisor, the second fraction, never the first one!
math/fraction-division.3bf6089bfbd2: Now four divided by two thirds. First cut every whole into thirds: twelve thirds in all. Each yellow piece is two thirds long, so twelve divided by two equals six pieces fit.
math/fraction-division.c955c7f93ad0: Another way to see it: dividing by two over three is two moves. How many thirds? Multiply by three, so three becomes nine thirds. How many groups of two thirds? Divide by two. Together: times three over two, the reciprocal of two over three.
math/fraction-division.2d3b22653eda: Worked example: you have two and a half cups of rice and one serving is three quarters of a cup. Five over two, divided by three over four, equals five over two, times four over three, equals twenty over six equals three and a third: three full servings and a third of another.
math/fraction-division.9b37935f6272: Same question with a fraction: four divided by one half, how many halves fit in four? Every whole holds two halves, so four wholes hold eight. Dividing by one half gives more, not less!
math/fraction-division.a46e59f053fc: Start with whole numbers. Six divided by two asks: how many twos fit in six? Lay pieces of length two under a bar of length six. Three fit, so six divided by two equals three.
math/fraction-division.6ea600202035: When the piece is bigger than what you have, not even one piece fits. One half divided by three quarters: the half fills only two of the three quarters in a piece, so the answer is one half times four thirds equals two thirds of a piece.

math/functions.730aa9ece4fd: Now plot each input-output pair from our machine as a point, x, y. They line up! Inputs in between work too: “two point five maps to six” lands on the same line. The graph is a picture of the whole function.
math/functions.783ee11879ec: Compare y equals x squared. Its outputs zero, one, four, nine jump by plus one, plus three, plus five: the rate of change keeps growing, so the graph bends. That is a nonlinear function. Equal steps in x with equal jumps in y means linear.
math/functions.9092bbecd864: Name it: a function gives each input exactly one output. For y equals two x plus one, every step of one to the right goes up two: the rate of change is two, and the starting value, at x equals zero, is one. A constant rate makes a straight line: a linear function.
math/functions.a14950c5e0c2: Not every rule is a function. "Give me a number whose square is x" sends four to both two and minus two: one input, two outputs, so it is NOT a function. But two inputs sharing one output, like negative two, all squared equals two squared equals four, is perfectly fine.
math/functions.6e1da518dc86: Common mix-up: Two different inputs sharing the same output is fine, two and minus two both square to four, and it is still a function. What is NOT allowed is one input with two or more different outputs.
math/functions.cf9db2f1e416: Meet a machine. Whatever number you drop in, it doubles it and then adds one. Drop in three… out comes seven.
math/functions.e7138db7d164: Worked example: a plant is three, five, seven, nine centimeters tall in weeks zero to three. It grows plus two centimeters each week, rate of change two, starting at three centimeters, so h equals two w plus three. In week ten: h equals two times ten plus three equals twenty-three centimeters.
math/functions.40e74d813bf2: Graphs tell stories. Here distance from home is a function of time: walking away, rising, stopped to chat, flat, rate zero, running, steeper equals faster, then walking home, falling, negative rate.

math/integers.5c3b631c888e: At three p.m. it is six degrees Celsius. Overnight the air cools to zero degrees Celsius, and keeps falling. By dawn it is four degrees below zero. We write that as minus four degrees Celsius: a negative number.
math/integers.64772ebba59d: The three rules in one place. Opposites: a and negative a are the same distance from zero. Absolute value: the absolute value of a is that distance, so the absolute value of a equals the absolute value of negative a. Order: a is less than b exactly when a is to the left of b.
math/integers.fb516a2facb9: Watch out: negative six has the larger absolute value, because it is farther from zero. But it is the smaller number. Being farther left always means smaller, no matter how far from zero.
math/integers.ba4003578fb0: On a number line, numbers get greater as you move right. Negative two is to the right of negative six, so negative two is greater than negative six. Think temperature: minus two degrees Celsius is warmer than minus six degrees Celsius.
math/integers.a01b1c2bbe85: Worked example: order negative five, three, negative one, zero, negative seven, six from least to greatest. Drop each number onto the line, then read from left to right: negative seven is less than negative five is less than negative one is less than zero is less than three is less than six.
math/integers.ffbe2766d48e: The absolute value of a is a number’s distance from zero. Negative five is five steps from zero, so the absolute value of negative five equals five; and the absolute value of five equals five too. A distance is never negative.
math/integers.36cbf21993de: Common mix-up: minus six looks like it has the “bigger number”, but it is LESS than minus two: on a number line, farther left means smaller. Minus six has the larger absolute value, which only means it is farther from zero, not that it is greater.
math/integers.12fd38150c7e: Turn the vertical scale on its side and you get a number line that keeps going left of zero. Positive numbers are to the right of zero, negative numbers to the left, and zero itself is neither.
math/integers.aee68b499e1a: Negative numbers describe the opposite direction from a zero point. Sea level is zero: a bird three meters above it is at plus three, a fish four meters below it is at negative four. Money works the same way: owing five dollars is negative five.
math/integers.afb0b220fc90: Three and negative three are the same distance from zero, on opposite sides. They are opposites: fold the line at zero and one lands on the other. The opposite of negative three is the negative of negative three, equals three.

math/inverse-proportion.eb2f32bc3299: In direct proportion, the ratio y over x is constant for nonzero x, and the full graph is a line through the origin. In inverse proportion, the product x y is constant and the graph is a hyperbola. Double a positive x and the direct output doubles while the inverse output halves.
math/inverse-proportion.8fdab4df9d91: Distance equals average speed multiplied by travel time. With distance fixed at one hundred twenty kilometers, twice the average speed takes half the time.
math/inverse-proportion.069a2a75c48a: Set the two expressions equal. Since x is not equal to zero, you can multiply both sides by x. Substitute each valid x into either original equation to find y.
math/inverse-proportion.5e9ba0d781d8: Average pressure is perpendicular force divided by contact area. With force fixed at six hundred newtons, doubling the contact area halves the average pressure.
math/inverse-proportion.f2f346f9ee2b: If y equals k over x, where k is a fixed nonzero number and x is not equal to zero, then y varies inversely with x. The graph is a hyperbola. Its two branches get closer to the axes without touching them. The perpendiculars from P to the axes form a rectangle with side lengths the absolute value of x and the absolute value of y, so its area is the absolute value of x y equals the absolute value of k. To see whether y rises or falls as x increases, look at one branch at a time.

math/negative-operations.fea6367f222b: Same trick for three minus negative two: add two zero pairs, then take away two red chips: five yellow remain. Taking away negative two gives the same result as adding plus two. Subtracting is adding the opposite: a minus b equals a plus negative b.
math/negative-operations.b1bf4e5096c7: Division undoes multiplication, so it follows the same rules. Since negative two times negative three equals six, we get six divided by negative two equals negative three. Since negative two times three equals negative six, we get negative six divided by negative two equals three. Same signs: positive; different signs: negative.
math/negative-operations.865df104e7c6: Another picture: chips. A yellow chip is plus one, a red chip is negative one, and one of each makes a zero pair: plus one plus negative one equals zero. In five plus negative three, three zero pairs vanish and two yellow chips remain, so the answer is two.
math/negative-operations.2f40fe71b7a1: Another way to see it: multiplying by negative one flips a number to the other side of zero. Flip three once: negative three. Flip again: back to three. So negative two times negative three means stretch negative three to negative six, then flip: plus six.
math/negative-operations.efd76ac945ce: But what is negative one times negative two? “Negative one group” makes no sense, so follow the pattern. Each time the first factor goes down by one, the answer goes UP by two. Keep going past zero: two, four, six. So a negative times a negative is positive!
math/negative-operations.d178979e7105: Adding means moving along the number line. Three plus four: start at three and step four to the right, landing on seven. Adding a negative steps LEFT: three plus negative five lands on negative two.
math/negative-operations.2e30e061c238: Put it together: negative two times three minus negative five. Multiply first: three jumps of negative two reach negative six. Then subtracting negative five means adding five: walk right five to land on negative one.
math/negative-operations.a7736f0ea5d6: Multiplication counts equal groups. Three times two is three groups of two yellow chips: six. Three times negative two is three groups of two red chips: negative six. A positive times a negative is negative.
math/negative-operations.b554b22f248c: Common mix-up: “Two negatives make a positive” is a rule for multiplying and dividing only! Adding is different: minus three plus minus four equals minus seven, two negatives added get MORE negative. And minus five minus three is minus eight, not minus two: subtracting three walks three more steps left.
math/negative-operations.18957584c2ea: Subtraction means take away. Five minus two: remove two yellow chips and three are left. But two minus five? There are only two to take! Add three zero pairs, that adds zero, so the value is still two, then take away five yellow chips: three red remain, so two minus five equals negative three.

math/percents.f3b3169b3684: So a percent of a number is just a multiplication: thirty percent of eighty is thirty over one hundred times eighty equals zero point three times eighty equals twenty-four. In words: part equals percent times whole.
math/percents.3459639b649d: A sixty-dollar jacket is twenty-five percent off. The discount is a quarter of the price: fifteen dollars. You pay the other seventy-five percent: sixty times the quantity one minus zero point two five equals sixty times zero point seven five equals forty-five dollars.
math/percents.aab35866297a: Now add eight percent sales tax to the forty-five dollars. The forty-five becomes the new one hundred percent, and the bar grows to one hundred eight percent: forty-five times one point zero eight equals forty-eight dollars and sixty cents. An increase of p means multiply by the quantity one plus p.
math/percents.938f28d2e90f: A few benchmarks are worth knowing by heart. Fifty percent is half the grid, twenty-five percent is a quarter, ten percent is one column, and one percent is a single square.
math/percents.87b8060dfe8c: A percent bar lines the whole up with one hundred percent. To find thirty percent of eighty, cut the bar into ten equal parts. Each part is ten percent, worth eighty divided by ten equals eight. Three parts make three times eight equals twenty-four.
math/percents.a2a0e8932a7a: Common mix-up: A percent is always a percent OF some whole. Going up twenty percent and then down twenty percent does not bring you back: the second twenty percent is taken of the bigger new price, one hundred, one hundred twenty, ninety-six.
math/percents.1df31c8a7995: Now work backwards: twelve is forty percent of what number? Forty percent is four parts, so one part, ten percent, is twelve divided by four equals three. The whole is ten parts: ten times three equals thirty.
math/percents.dd6c2b2b5341: Careful! A price of one hundred goes up twenty percent to one hundred twenty, then down twenty percent. The second twenty percent is taken of one hundred twenty, so it removes twenty-four: one hundred twenty times zero point eight equals ninety-six. You do not get back to one hundred!
math/percents.9dd3bf90a97b: Percent means "per hundred". Here are one hundred equal squares. Shade thirty-seven of them and you have shaded thirty-seven over one hundred of the grid: that is thirty-seven percent.
math/percents.cf1a69467bcf: The whole is not always one hundred. In a class of twenty, twenty-five percent walk to school. Twenty-five percent is one over four: one out of every four students. Five groups of four give five walkers.

math/probability.14552560f3b6: Flip two coins. A tree diagram lists every outcome: H H, H T, T H and T T, four equally likely outcomes. One head and one tail happens in two of them, so its probability is two over four equals one over two, not one over three.
math/probability.a530554541c3: The key ideas: every probability is between zero and one. With equally likely outcomes, P equals favourable over total. And the chance that something does not happen is one minus P: for example, the probability of not rolling a six is one minus one over six equals five over six.
math/probability.369c004b5432: A fair die has six equally likely outcomes. Three of them are even: two, four and six. So the probability of rolling an even number is three over six equals one over two. Count the favourable outcomes, then divide by all the equally likely outcomes.
math/probability.8d8c7e251c98: Common mix-up: A coin has no memory: after five heads in a row, the next flip is still one half heads. And two coins have four equally likely outcomes, H H, H T, T H, T T, not three, so "one head and one tail" has probability one half, not one third.
math/probability.36ba71a80cf2: A bag holds three red, five blue and two green marbles. P of blue equals five over ten equals one over two and P of not red equals one minus three over ten equals seven over ten. Draw two hundred times, putting the marble back each time, and expect about two hundred times one over two equals one hundred blues.
math/probability.caf692bba967: Keep flipping: one hundred, one thousand, then ten thousand times. At first the fraction of heads jumps around, but as the flips pile up it settles closer and closer to zero point five. This is the law of large numbers: with many trials, experimental probability approaches theoretical probability.
math/probability.a9846db8bb04: Probability helps us predict. Roll a die six hundred times: we expect each number about six hundred times one over six equals one hundred times. The real counts land close to one hundred, but rarely exactly on it.
math/probability.68afe681cb68: Probability measures how likely something is, on a scale from zero, impossible, to one, certain. Rolling a seven on a normal die is impossible, a coin landing heads is an even chance, one over two, and rolling a number from one to six is certain.
math/probability.a5d2015880b9: Roll two dice. A six by six table shows all thirty-six equally likely outcomes. A total of seven can happen in six ways, more than any other total, so P of seven equals six over thirty-six equals one over six. A total of two happens in only one way.
math/probability.f5b03b13c81e: Theory says heads should come up half the time. Let's really flip a coin ten times. Seven heads! The experimental probability is seven over ten equals zero point seven, not zero point five. Is the theory wrong?

math/proportional.ec90e8079753: A hiker walks at a steady pace. After one hour she has gone three kilometers, after two hours six kilometers, after three hours nine kilometers, and after four hours twelve kilometers. Let's record it in a table.
math/proportional.28ceac4ed9ca: Walk along the line in steps: every one hour to the right, the line climbs three kilometers. The point, one, three, shows the unit rate: three kilometers for ONE hour. That number is the constant of proportionality, k equals three.
math/proportional.70523900847c: Compare a taxi: four dollars just to get in, then two dollars per mile. The ratios six over one, eight over two, ten over three, twelve over four keep changing, and the line starts at zero, four, not at the origin. Being a straight line is not enough: y equals two x plus four is NOT proportional.
math/proportional.8f1cb4d20c20: Table, graph and equation are three views of the same relationship: y equals three x. In general, a proportional relationship is y equals k x, where k equals y over x is the unit rate, the constant of proportionality.
math/proportional.56f7000448f2: Divide each distance by its time: three over one, six over two, nine over three, twelve over four. Every row gives the same number, three. When the ratio y over x never changes, we say y is proportional to x.
math/proportional.ff3caa1a0246: Change k and the line turns around the origin. A slower hiker, k equals one point five, gives a flatter line; a faster one, k equals five, a steeper line. Every one of them still passes through zero, zero.
math/proportional.4f9cc78bde27: Try it: five pounds of rice cost seven dollars and fifty cents. Unit rate: k equals seven point five zero divided by five equals one dollar and fifty cents per pound, so y equals one point five x. Then eight pounds cost one point five times eight equals twelve dollars.
math/proportional.77e629dd2b67: Extend the line backwards. At zero hours she has walked zero kilometers, so the line passes through the origin, zero, zero. A proportional relationship always graphs as a straight line through the origin.
math/proportional.d81697efeaf5: Common mix-up: A straight line does NOT automatically mean proportional! y equals two x plus four is a straight line too, but it misses the origin and y over x keeps changing. Proportional means BOTH: a straight line AND it passes through zero, zero.

math/pythagorean.d63f0ae90e72: Use it! A right triangle has legs six and eight. Then c squared equals thirty-six plus sixty-four equals one hundred, so c equals the square root of one hundred equals ten. The theorem turns two lengths into the third.
math/pythagorean.8f351d313b88: Try a three-four-five triangle and count unit squares: three squared equals nine and four squared equals sixteen. The big square holds five squared equals twenty-five, and nine plus sixteen equals twenty-five. Coincidence? Let's find out why it always works.

math/quadratic-equations.02eb498fae55: Move all terms to the left and combine like terms. A polynomial equation with one variable is quadratic when the highest power left is two. Its real roots are the x-values that make the left side zero. On the parabola, those are the x-intercepts. The discriminant is four. Two intercepts, crosses the axis twice
math/quadratic-equations.4691002bdf7d: Move all terms to the left and combine like terms. A polynomial equation with one variable is quadratic when the highest power left is two. Its real roots are the x-values that make the left side zero. On the parabola, those are the x-intercepts. The discriminant is negative eight. Zero intercepts, misses the axis

math/quadratic-functions.77c592808674: In vertex form y equals a times the quantity x minus h, squared, plus k, the square vanishes at x equals h. Move h and k and compare the solid curve with the dashed reference y equals a x squared.
math/quadratic-functions.56b7ed64c9b1: Find the allowed inputs first. If both endpoints are allowed, compare their outputs with the vertex's output if the vertex is in the domain. If an endpoint is excluded, the function may approach an extreme value without ever reaching it. Use all twenty-four meters of fencing on three sides of a rectangle beside a wall. Drag the point to change the depth x in meters and see how the area A in square meters changes. Open circles show the limits where no rectangle forms. A ball launches straight up from the ground at twenty meters per second. The model ignores air resistance and rounds the acceleration due to gravity to ten meters per second squared. Drag the point or move the time slider to see the height H in meters at time t in seconds.
math/quadratic-functions.96df3d4e89f3: A quadratic function has the form y equals a x squared plus b x plus c with a is not equal to zero. Its graph is a parabola. Change only c and watch the point on the y-axis. The two sides of the parabola mirror each other across its axis. When it opens up, y falls as x increases to the left of the vertex and rises to the right. When it opens down, the pattern reverses. Set x equals zero to find the y-intercept. Solve y equals zero to find the x-intercepts. Changing only c moves the whole graph up or down by the same amount.

math/radicals.ba7a5635fb30: Split the square into a six by six grid. There are thirty-six equal squares. Each has area seventy-two divided by thirty-six equals two.
math/radicals.91a0bee66b72: The area is seventy-two, so each side has length the square root of seventy-two.
math/radicals.d4209a11f6aa: In simplest radical form, there is no denominator inside the radical and no square factor left to take out. For a positive integer radicand, check for perfect-square factors greater than one. For example, three times the square root of eight simplifies to six times the square root of two. If the radicand is a perfect square, write the whole-number result, as in the square root of forty-nine equals seven.
math/radicals.3a92d144eb92: In the real numbers, an expression of the form the square root of a, with a is greater than or equal to zero, is a square-root expression. The symbol the square root of a means the principal square root of a, the nonnegative number whose square is a. The expression a under the radical sign is the radicand.
math/radicals.39921b61205a: Enter a whole number and test a perfect-square divisor. For example, seventy-two divided by thirty-six equals two. Divide the square of area seventy-two into six rows and six columns. Each small square has area two. Count along an edge to see the length of the big square.
math/radicals.08e55e6f63b1: Lift out a copy of the bottom row. Its six lengths of the square root of two add to six times the square root of two, so the square root of seventy-two equals six times the square root of two.

math/rational-expressions.2ac6c4d4138a: In English, a rational expression is one polynomial divided by another. Its denominator cannot be an expression that is always zero. The Chinese textbook term 分式 also requires a variable in the denominator. Exclude every value that makes the original denominator zero, even after reducing.
math/rational-expressions.4c425204a224: Each bar has one shaded piece. The two pieces have different sizes. Finding a common denominator, 通分, gives the fractions equal-sized pieces. Split a half and a third into x smaller pieces each and take one small piece from each. The denominators are now two x and three x, so use six x as their least common denominator. Here six is the least common multiple of two and three.
math/rational-expressions.935fa063558e: Divide out the common factor. Divide both products by x plus three. Keep minus three excluded because the original denominator is zero there.
math/rational-expressions.33475e0d5d4e: Each bar now has six equal pieces. The shaded lengths stay the same. Finding a common denominator, 通分, gives the fractions equal-sized pieces. Split a half and a third into x smaller pieces each and take one small piece from each. The denominators are now two x and three x, so use six x as their least common denominator. Here six is the least common multiple of two and three.
math/rational-expressions.029dde235b33: A rational equation has an unknown in a denominator. Exclude values that make an original denominator zero. Multiply every term on both sides by the least common denominator, then solve the resulting equation. Substitute each candidate into the original equation. If a candidate makes a denominator zero, it is an extraneous solution, 增根.
math/rational-expressions.0b96dd363ace: Given that A can finish the job alone in six hours, how long would B take alone? Each worker keeps the same rate alone or together. Move the slider to change the time they take together.
math/rational-expressions.673e30eb28d5: The top and middle shade the same length. Move left to divide out the common factor and return to one half. Split every piece into the same number of smaller pieces. The shaded length stays the same. Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same polynomial. The fraction keeps its value wherever that factor is nonzero. To reduce, 约分, divide out a common factor. Let x count the smaller pieces made from each piece of the top bar. In the diagram x is a positive integer. The equation below holds for every nonzero real x.

math/ratios.7aaba1690d3a: Stretch the tapes into a double number line: blue on top, yellow below. Each jump adds one more batch, two cups of blue and three of yellow. Any two numbers lined up vertically make the same green.
math/ratios.397c46c561a4: How much yellow goes with one cup of blue? Halve both: two to three equals one to one point five. That is the unit rate: one point five cups of yellow per cup of blue. Now any amount is easy: seven cups of blue need seven times one point five equals ten point five cups of yellow.
math/ratios.6a06752cf2b0: Need more paint? Mix a second batch: now it is four to six. A third batch gives six to nine. The amounts grow together, and the colour stays exactly the same. These are equivalent ratios.
math/ratios.89de0473dc90: Worked example: a car goes one hundred fifty miles in three hours. How far in five hours? Find the rate for one hour, one hundred fifty divided by three equals fifty miles per hour, then scale up: five times fifty equals two hundred fifty miles.
math/ratios.25c70535b8ce: In a ratio table, go from two to three, to eight to twelve by multiplying both numbers by four: same shape, same green. But adding four to both gives six to seven. Yellow is no longer one point five times blue, so the colour changes!
math/ratios.60f5755ffdac: Squeeze each row into a tape diagram: blue is two equal parts, yellow is three, so five parts in all. For fifteen cups of paint, each part is fifteen divided by five equals three cups, so we need six cups of blue and nine cups of yellow.
math/ratios.a12f90c5b175: Plot each pair as a point, blue, yellow. Equivalent ratios all land on one straight line through zero: every two steps right, three steps up. Each pair gives the same quotient three over two equals one point five, the unit rate.
math/ratios.c10940fd226d: Common mix-up: To get an equivalent ratio you must MULTIPLY, or divide, both numbers by the same number. Adding the same amount to both, like two to three, three to four, changes the relationship, and the paint changes colour.
math/ratios.30867065e1d3: Unit rates settle shopping questions. Store A sells three notebooks for seven dollars and fifty cents; store B sells five for eleven dollars. Price of one: A is seven point five zero divided by three equals two point five zero, B is eleven divided by five equals two point two zero. Store B is the better buy.
math/ratios.ca72f05f39df: Here is a recipe for green paint: two cups of blue for every three cups of yellow. A ratio compares two amounts like this. We write two to three and read it "two to three".

math/roots-irrationals.37eb1b0b5a07: A square garden has an area of twenty-five square metres. How long is each side?
math/roots-irrationals.8b6f0054d74e: Squares of whole numbers, one, four, nine, sixteen, twenty-five, and so on are called perfect squares. Their square roots are whole numbers: the sides one, two, three, four, five.
math/roots-irrationals.a34af6a041d8: The same idea works in three D. A cube with volume twenty-seven has edge three, because three times three times three equals twenty-seven. So the cube root is the cube root of twenty-seven equals three.
math/roots-irrationals.921a59712d47: Count along the bottom: five tiles, because five times five equals twenty-five. The side length is the square root of the area: the square root of twenty-five equals five, since five squared equals twenty-five.
math/roots-irrationals.20da7310018c: How long is the square root of two? Swing the diagonal down onto the number line. Since one squared equals one is less than two is less than four equals two squared, it must land between one and two.
math/roots-irrationals.60f19386b20e: Worked example: solve x squared equals forty, so x equals plus or minus the square root of forty. Since thirty-six is less than forty is less than forty-nine, the square root of forty is between six and seven, and closer to six. Check: six point three squared equals thirty-nine point six nine, so the square root of forty is about six point three.
math/roots-irrationals.bf3624328e3f: Fractions behave differently: their decimals either end, one over four equals zero point two five, or repeat, one over seven equals zero point one four two eight five seven. Those are rational numbers. Numbers like the square root of two and pi cannot be written as a fraction: they are irrational.
math/roots-irrationals.5457f6d9d683: Zoom in. One point four squared equals one point nine six is a bit less than two, and one point five squared equals two point two five is more, so the square root of two is between one point four and one point five. The first decimal digit is four.
math/roots-irrationals.10f30bc7990d: Common mix-up: the square root of two is not one point four one or even one point four one four: those are only approximations, and its decimal never ends. Also, a square root is not "divide by two": the square root of sixteen equals four, not eight. The equation x squared equals sixteen has two solutions, x equals plus or minus four, but the symbol the square root of sixteen means only the positive one.
math/roots-irrationals.0acc31ef5286: Now a puzzle: which square has area two? Cut two unit squares along their diagonals and slide two halves down. The four pieces form a tilted square of area two, so its side is the square root of two: the diagonal of a unit square.
math/roots-irrationals.2d089ebea93a: Keep zooming: one point four one, then one point four one four, … Every zoom reveals one more digit, and it never stops: the square root of two equals one point four one four two one three five six and so on. The digits never end and never settle into a repeating pattern.

math/sampling.5663facf613b: Comparing two groups: plant heights without, A, and with, B, fertilizer, ten random plants each. Mean A equals eleven centimeters, mean B equals fifteen centimeters, and both have a mean absolute deviation, MAD, of one point four centimeters. The centers differ by four centimeters, almost three MADs, so the two piles overlap only a little: the fertilizer really seems to help.
math/sampling.694751fc72ce: Here is a jar of three hundred beads, some of them red. The whole jar is the population. What fraction is red? We could count every bead, but for a real population, every voter in a country, every fish in a lake, that is impossible.
math/sampling.d024f2a19434: Now use bigger samples of eighty beads each. The new pile is much narrower: bigger samples vary less, so a single big sample is more likely to land close to the truth.
math/sampling.16b471ff598b: Worked example: in a random sample of fifty students from a school of six hundred, eighteen named soccer as their favourite sport. Sample proportion: eighteen over fifty equals thirty-six percent. Estimate for the whole school: zero point three six times six hundred equals two hundred sixteen students. It is an estimate, not an exact count.
math/sampling.8886bddc6a05: Repeat it forty times. Each dot is one random sample of twenty beads, placed at its percentage of red. The dots pile up into a hill: most samples land near the middle, but some are far off.
math/sampling.889b22dee633: Reveal the truth: ninety of the three hundred beads are red, exactly thirty percent. Both piles are centered near thirty percent. That is inference: the proportion in a random sample is a fair estimate of the proportion in the population.
math/sampling.d490c19f776d: But beware of bias. These red beads were poured in last and the jar was never shaken, so they sit near the top. Grab the twenty beads on top and seventeen are red: eighty-five percent! When not every bead has an equal chance, the sample is biased, and repeating it never fixes that.
math/sampling.5ffffdf7e8e6: Instead, take a random sample: shake the jar and pull out twenty beads without looking, so every bead has the same chance of being picked. This handful has six red out of twenty, so we estimate p hat equals six over twenty equals thirty percent red.
math/sampling.1d0264806707: Put them back, shake, and draw again. This time nine of twenty are red: forty-five percent. Two random samples, two different answers! This natural wobble from sample to sample is called sampling variability.

math/scale-drawings.67cbead2a2a0: What if we stretch only the width? Now eight divided by four equals two but three divided by three equals one. The house looks squashed, so this is not a scale drawing. Every length must use the same factor.
math/scale-drawings.2386e217775f: Here is a little house drawn on graph paper. Its wall is four squares wide and three squares tall. How can we draw it bigger without changing its shape?
math/scale-drawings.cd63410f892a: Multiply every length by the same number. Here each length doubles: four becomes eight and three becomes six. That number is the scale factor, k equals two.
math/scale-drawings.aa173e87c388: Now area. A three by two rectangle covers six squares. Scale it by k equals two: every square becomes a two by two block of four squares, so the area becomes four times six equals twenty-four, not twelve!
math/scale-drawings.d8888f9630ed: Maps are scale drawings too. On this map one centimeter stands for five kilometers. The road from A to B measures five centimeters, so the real distance is five times five equals twenty-five kilometers.
math/scale-drawings.5f517984effe: A scale factor less than one shrinks the drawing. With k equals one over two, four becomes two and three becomes one point five. If k is greater than one it is an enlargement; if k is less than one it is a reduction.
math/scale-drawings.6aa0fa74fb91: With k equals three, each square becomes a three by three block of nine squares, so the area is nine times six equals fifty-four. Lengths grow by k, but areas grow by k times k equals k squared.
math/scale-drawings.790948d47251: Common mix-up: Lengths multiply by the scale factor k, but areas multiply by k squared. Triple the sides and the area becomes nine times as big, not three times. And stretching in only one direction is not scaling: the shape changes.
math/scale-drawings.5daa560b4ae2: Try it! A floor plan uses the scale one centimeter to two meters. A room is four centimeters by three centimeters on the plan, so it is really eight meters by six meters, with area forty-eight square meters. Check: twelve times two squared equals forty-eight.

math/scatter-plots.dd82e5b7e17c: Look for points that break the pattern. This student studied six hours but scored only forty-five, maybe sick on test day: an outlier. A group of points bunched together is a cluster: many students studied two to three hours.
math/scatter-plots.9aee6842b857: Use it to predict. A new student plans to study four hours. Go up from four to the line, then across: y equals five point five times four plus fifty-three equals seventy-five. We predict a score of about seventy-five.
math/scatter-plots.3e8d3cadb47c: Turn every pair into a point. Hours go across on the x-axis and the score goes up on the y-axis, so the student with zero point five, fifty-five, lands here. Do it for all twelve and we get a scatter plot.
math/scatter-plots.c5137117dfd6: But be careful far outside the data. Stretch the line to ten hours and it predicts one hundred eight points, more than the maximum of one hundred! A trend line is trustworthy only near the data that made it.
math/scatter-plots.6f04dc691038: Read the line like any linear function: y equals five point five x plus fifty-three. The slope five point five says each extra hour of study goes with about five point five more points. The y-intercept fifty-three is the predicted score for zero hours.

math/similar-triangles.2c15a7b57fae: Angles A and D are both sixty-five degrees. Change angle E to match angle B. Write a similarity statement in matching vertex order. In A B C is similar to D E F, A matches D, B matches E, and C matches F, so A B matches D E, and so on.
math/similar-triangles.506d10948291: Two ratios are fixed at one point five. Change E F until the third side ratio matches. Write a similarity statement in matching vertex order. In A B C is similar to D E F, A matches D, B matches E, and C matches F, so A B matches D E, and so on.
math/similar-triangles.29b25fa116f9: Draw a line through the center O and each vertex. Multiply each distance from O by the same positive number k. In Basic mode, each image vertex stays on the same ray from O as its original. Corresponding angles match, and every side length scales by k. Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. Perimeter is the sum of the sides, so it scales by k. The base and the height each scale by k, so area scales by k squared. When k equals one, the triangles are congruent and similar.

math/slope.6a88e19923f1: Start at a point on the line and walk to another one: three squares right, the run, then two squares up, the rise. We land back on the line.
math/slope.f55212ebce12: Where does the line start? It crosses the y-axis at the y-intercept b equals one. From there every three steps right add two, so y equals two over three, times x plus one. In general: y equals m x plus b
math/slope.83df4dda4333: If the line falls as you move right, the rise is negative, so the slope is negative. A horizontal line has rise zero, so m equals zero. A vertical line has run zero, and rise over zero is undefined.
math/slope.f1ad4c294017: A bigger slope makes a steeper line; a slope close to zero makes a flatter one. Watch the triangle, run two, rise two m, stretch as m changes.
math/slope.7239a1bd26e0: Common mix-up: Slope is rise divided by run, vertical change divided by horizontal change, not the other way round. Subtract the y's and the x's in the same order. And keep these apart: a horizontal line has slope zero, but a vertical line's slope is undefined, you cannot divide by zero.
math/slope.7f787f74fb5d: That unchanging ratio is the slope, written m: m equals rise over run equals Delta y over Delta x equals y sub two minus y sub one, over x sub two minus x sub one. For our line m equals two over three: each one step right, it rises two over three.
math/slope.f4d68686c726: Worked example: find the line through one, three, and three, seven. Slope: m equals seven minus three, over three minus one, equals four over two equals two. Put one point in: three equals two times one plus b, so b equals one. The line is y equals two x plus one.
math/slope.e342d82ab024: Do it again, and again. From anywhere on the line, three right and two up lands you back on the line. The staircase steps are all identical.
math/slope.90c4f7166e3a: Now take a big step, six right, four up, and a tiny one, one point five right, one up. Different sizes, same shape: the triangles are similar, with the same angle. So the ratio rise divided by run never changes.

math/statistics.419c64db6afb: Try it with four, eight, six, five, seven. Mean: thirty divided by five equals six. In order four, five, six, seven, eight, so the median is six. Range: eight minus four equals four. MAD: the quantity two plus one plus zero plus one plus two, divided by five equals one point two.
math/statistics.cfab865334af: Five friends count the books they read this month: two, seven, four, three and nine. One read a lot, one read very little. What single number fairly describes the “typical” amount?
math/statistics.af2caf317159: Center is not the whole story; we also want spread. The range is max minus min: nine minus two equals seven. The mean absolute deviation, MAD, is the average distance from the mean: line the distances up, three plus two plus one plus two plus four equals twelve, then share them out, twelve divided by five equals two point four.
math/statistics.f3566dbbe454: The median is the middle value once the data are in order. Cross off one value from each end, again and again: two and nine, then three and seven. The one left, four, is the median. With an even number of values, take the halfway point of the two middle ones.
math/statistics.14178858a10a: Now put the same data on a number line as a dot plot. The mean is also the balance point: the distances on the left, three plus two plus one equals six, exactly match the distances on the right, two plus four equals six, so the line balances at five.
math/statistics.b83608705758: Common mix-up: Always put the data in order before finding the median! For seven, two, nine the median is seven, in order: two, seven, nine, not the two that happens to sit in the middle of the list. And the mean and median are not always equal: an outlier drags the mean toward it.
math/statistics.490ff6768a97: Idea: share the books out evenly. Move books from tall stacks to short ones until every stack is level. Everyone ends up with five, because the total, twenty-five, split five ways is twenty-five divided by five equals five. That level is the mean.

math/surface-volume.44e966b3bb07: The box is two units tall, so that layer repeats two times: twelve times two equals twenty-four cubes. The volume is twenty-four units cubed.
math/surface-volume.993b489549d3: Here is a box, a rectangular prism: four units long, three units wide and two units tall. How much space is inside it? To measure space, we first need a measuring tool.
math/surface-volume.75d6253a2c6e: Now fill a box that is two by one and a half by one with these half-size cubes: four times three times two equals twenty-four of them. Twenty-four times one eighth equals three, exactly what two times one and a half times one gives. The formula still works!
math/surface-volume.019a3ac98e36: A different question: how much paper covers the box? That is the surface area, the total area of all six faces. Cut along some edges and lay the box flat: this flat pattern is called a net.
math/surface-volume.7e27fb4dd858: What if an edge is a fraction, like one and a half? Cut a unit cube in half along every edge: you get eight small cubes with edge one half. Each is one eighth of the unit cube, and indeed one half times one half times one half equals one eighth.
math/surface-volume.ae3a9a1fa497: Try it: a cereal box is eight centimeters wide, three centimeters deep and twelve centimeters tall. V equals eight times three times twelve equals two hundred eighty-eight centimeters cubed of cereal fits inside, and S A equals two times the quantity twenty-four plus ninety-six plus thirty-six, equals three hundred twelve centimeters squared of cardboard wraps it.
math/surface-volume.04411a0976c3: Our measuring tool is the unit cube: every edge is one unit long. Its volume is one cubic unit, one unit cubed. Volume equals how many unit cubes it takes to fill a shape.
math/surface-volume.4f8c0546aa93: Fill the floor first. The bottom is four by three, so one layer holds four times three equals twelve cubes. That number is the area of the base: B equals twelve.
math/surface-volume.c808f508c551: The faces come in matching pairs: two four times three, two four times two, two three times two. Count the squares: two times twelve plus two times eight plus two times six equals fifty-two units squared. In general, S A equals two times the quantity l w plus l h plus w h.

math/systems.541fa06a5f14: A puzzle: you buy seven snacks and spend exactly ten dollars. Cookies cost one dollar each and juice boxes cost two dollars each. Call the number of cookies x and juice boxes y. A first guess, three cookies and four juice boxes, costs eleven dollars, too much!
math/systems.d4f59e40745c: Graphs can be hard to read exactly, so we also solve with algebra. Substitution: clue one says x equals seven minus y. Put that in place of x in clue two: seven minus y, plus two y equals ten, so y equals three, and then x equals four.
math/systems.80e44f7695e1: Which guess fits both clues? Only the point on both lines: where they cross, four, three. Check: four plus three equals seven and four plus two times three equals ten. So you bought four cookies and three juice boxes.
math/systems.06a3a7c0b948: Now use only the second clue, the cost: one dollar per cookie and two dollars per juice box gives x plus two y equals ten. Its guesses, zero, five; two, four; four, three… also line up, on a different line.
math/systems.52005c993e49: Elimination: stack the two clues as bars. Clue two has everything clue one has plus one more y, and its total is ten minus seven equals three bigger. Subtracting the equations cancels x and leaves y equals three.
math/systems.c291ed75eb13: Worked example: adult tickets cost five dollars, child tickets three dollars, and ten tickets cost thirty-eight dollars. Multiply the first equation by three and subtract: y cancels, leaving two x equals eight, so x equals four adults and y equals six children. Always check in both equations!
math/systems.1646152723e5: Use only the first clue, seven items: x plus y equals seven. Try every guess: zero cookies and seven juice boxes, one and six, two and five… Plot each guess as a point, x, y. They all land on one straight line!

math/transformations.0e435c9b19c9: Common mix-up: A ninety-degree counterclockwise rotation about the origin is x, y to minus y, x, not minus x, y; that one is a reflection across the y-axis. And a dilated figure is similar to the original but not congruent, unless the scale factor k equals one.
math/transformations.c502e6b73184: A dilation resizes. With center zero, zero, and scale factor k equals one point five, every point slides along its ray from the origin until it is one point five times as far: x, y to one point five x, one point five y. A factor k equals one half shrinks it instead.
math/transformations.0d08803c4530: Rotation, a turn, by ninety degrees counterclockwise about the origin. Follow B, four, one: it swings around to B prime, negative one, four. The coordinates swap places and the new first one changes sign: x, y to negative y, x.
math/transformations.08fa4b8b2c13: Worked example: which moves take A B C onto the pink triangle? It is upside down, so first reflect across the x-axis: x, y to x, negative y. Then slide six left: x, y to x minus six, y. Together: x, y to x minus six, negative y. Only rigid motions, so the triangles are congruent.
math/transformations.e7192bfdf74f: Translation, a slide: every point moves six left and four down. Watch the coordinates of A change: subtract six from x and four from y. Rule: x, y to x minus six, y minus four.
math/transformations.dca5d049467b: Here is triangle A B C on the coordinate grid: A, two, one. B, four, one. C, two, two. A transformation moves every point of a shape by the same rule. Let us slide it, flip it, turn it and resize it, and track the coordinates.
math/transformations.b229b9a73fd9: Compare the shapes. The angles stay the same, the right angle is still a right angle, and every side is multiplied by the same factor: three over two equals one point five over one equals one point five. Same shape, different size: similar, is similar to, not congruent.

math/trig-ratios.e878621aab13: Draw the diagonal of a unit square. It splits a right angle in half, giving forty-five degrees. Both legs are one, so the Pythagorean theorem gives a diagonal of the square root of two.
math/trig-ratios.f7121a1252e7: Draw an altitude from the top of an equilateral triangle with side length two. It halves the sixty-degree top angle and the base. Each right triangle has a thirty-degree angle at the top and a sixty-degree angle at the base. The short leg is one. The other leg is the square root of the quantity two squared minus one squared equals the square root of three.

math/volume-solids.578c8ce6c270: Fill the sphere with water and pour it into the empty cylinder: it fills two thirds. The cone fills the last third. Cone to sphere to cylinder equals one to two to three, as Archimedes discovered over two thousand years ago.
math/volume-solids.e98fd9ff6080: Now stack twelve identical coins. Every layer has the same area pi r squared, and the layers pile up to a height h. So the volume of the stack is area of one layer times height.
math/volume-solids.9edc9ca1a5ac: Turn that into a formula. The sphere is two thirds of a cylinder with radius r and height two r: V sphere equals two thirds times pi r squared times two r equals four thirds times pi r cubed
math/volume-solids.6a65641cee85: So a cone holds one third of the cylinder with the same base and height: V cone equals one third times pi r squared h. A pyramid is one third of its prism for the same reason.
math/volume-solids.06065f2e72b9: Try it with r equals three centimeters and h equals six centimeters. Cylinder: fifty-four pi is about one hundred sixty-nine point six cubic centimeters. Cone: eighteen pi is about fifty-six point five cubic centimeters. Sphere: thirty-six pi is about one hundred thirteen point one cubic centimeters. And eighteen pi plus thirty-six pi equals fifty-four pi, just as the water showed.
math/volume-solids.57e673b2da8f: Now a ball, a sphere, of radius r. Our cylinder is exactly two r tall, so the ball fits perfectly inside: it touches the bottom, the top and the sides.
math/volume-solids.c60f05310ce0: Common mix-up: The formulas use the radius r, not the diameter, a ten centimeter diameter means r equals five centimeters. The height h of a cone is the straight-up height from the tip to the base, not the slanted length along its side.
math/volume-solids.78fe90911693: Let the water decide. Fill the cone, pour it into the cylinder, and repeat. It takes exactly three cones of water to fill the cylinder.

music/music-compose.90c0a43e2ac9: Motif. A tiny musical idea you can recognize. Often just two to six notes. Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony is built from a four-note motif: short, short, short, LONG.
music/music-compose.1854d64bfd00: Phrase. A musical sentence. Usually two or four bars long — about one breath of singing. Phrases end with a cadence, like sentences end with punctuation.
music/music-compose.5f8db4d43784: Chord and progression. Notes stacked together, then moving in order. A triad stacks one, three, five of a scale step. A progression is the order of chords — the song’s “road map.”
music/music-compose.55a13e60a7f5: Don't mix up: 起承转合 is about the shape of phrases, not a set of chords.
music/music-compose.33b3daf7a54c: 起承转合. The Chinese four-phrase plan. 起 begin, 承 continue, 转 turn, 合 close. Phrase two echoes phrase one, phrase three changes direction, phrase four brings it home. Many Chinese folk songs and poems follow it.

music/music-history.29f1d4e5c3ef: Film and game music. Nineteen thirties to today. Film scores use leitmotifs: a short theme for each character, an idea from Wagner’s operas. John Williams’ Star Wars, nineteen seventy-seven, brought back the full symphony orchestra to the movies. Today game music adapts live to what the player does.
music/music-history.977238634163: Peking opera and pipa classics. Seventeen ninety, eighteen eighteen. Seventeen ninety: four opera troupes from Anhui came to Beijing for the emperor’s birthday — the start of Peking opera 京剧. Peking opera combines singing, speech, acting and acrobatics, led by the percussion band. The pipa epic 十面埋伏, “Ambush from Ten Sides,” about the battle of Gaixia, two hundred two B C E, was first printed in a pipa book in eighteen eighteen.
music/music-history.40a3305e1c07: Classical. Seventeen fifty to eighteen twenty. Haydn, “father of the symphony,” Mozart and young Beethoven. Clear, balanced melodies over simple accompaniments — elegant, like neat architecture. New forms: the symphony, the string quartet and sonata form.
music/music-history.bc37f08427ed: Ragtime, blues and jazz. Eighteen nineties to nineteen forties. Created by African American musicians, drawing on spirituals, work songs and West African rhythm. Scott Joplin’s “Maple Leaf Rag,” eighteen ninety-nine; the twelve-bar blues with “blue notes.” The first jazz record came out in nineteen seventeen; Louis Armstrong made improvised solos the star. Swing big bands, Duke Ellington, followed.
music/music-history.372814656406: Romantic. Eighteen twenty to nineteen hundred. Big feelings, bigger orchestras. Beethoven’s late works open the door. Chopin’s piano poetry, Tchaikovsky’s ballets, The Nutcracker, eighteen ninety-two. Composers celebrated their nations’ folk music, Dvořák, Grieg.
music/music-history.aeef944a3e0b: Don't mix up: Modern “classical” composers are still writing today — it did not end in eighteen twenty.
music/music-history.207d17148e76: Twentieth-century classical. Nineteen hundred to today. Debussy’s dreamy whole-tone colours; Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring, nineteen thirteen, caused an uproar at its premiere in Paris. Composers broke old rules: new scales, wild rhythms, electronic sounds. Minimalists, Steve Reich, Philip Glass, built music from short repeating patterns.
music/music-history.f99d80685696: Hip-hop. Nineteen seventy-three to today. August eleventh, nineteen seventy-three, the Bronx, New York: DJ Kool Herc loops the drum “breaks” of records at a party. Four elements: DJing, MCing, rapping, breakdancing and graffiti. Drum machines like the Roland T R eight zero eight and sampling made new beats — the same step-sequencer idea as our Rhythm lesson.
music/music-history.ff1e814ce021: Don't mix up: Guqin, seven strings, no bridges, is not equal to guzheng, twenty-one strings, bridges.
music/music-history.750f65f3ae5a: Bronze bells and the guqin. Circa four hundred thirty-three B C E. The sixty-five bells of Marquis Yi of Zeng show China had a full twelve-note system two thousand four hundred years ago. The legend of 伯牙 Boya and 钟子期 Zhong Ziqi: Boya played 高山流水, “High Mountains, Flowing Water,” and only his friend understood it. A true friend is still called 知音 — “one who knows the sound.” The guqin piece 流水 flew into space on Voyager in nineteen seventy-seven.
music/music-history.3d634c9969b9: Tang dynasty music. Six hundred eighteen to nine hundred seven. Chang’an was a world city: music arrived along the Silk Road from Central Asia, including the pipa. Emperor Xuanzong ran a music academy, the 梨园 “Pear Garden” — Chinese opera performers are still nicknamed “children of the Pear Garden.” Grand suites called 大曲 mixed music, song and dance.
music/music-history.ade44123e01f: East meets West. Nineteen fifty-nine to today. 梁祝 The Butterfly Lovers violin concerto, nineteen fifty-nine, by 何占豪 He Zhanhao and 陈钢 Chen Gang, puts Yue-opera melodies into a Western concerto. Large Chinese orchestras, 民族管弦乐团, mix erhu, pipa, dizi and percussion. Tan Dun won the Oscar for best original score for Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, two thousand.
music/music-history.cec5b98e9150: Don't mix up: Baroque music used the harpsichord, not the modern piano, invented around seventeen hundred and common later.
music/music-history.6defa7a7dfbd: Baroque. Sixteen hundred to seventeen fifty. Opera is born in Italy around sixteen hundred. Bach, Vivaldi and Handel. Busy, interlocking melodies, counterpoint — like a fugue, where one tune chases itself. A harpsichord or organ plays the “basso continuo,” a non-stop bass line.
music/music-history.75424e62496d: New Chinese music. Nineteen twenties to nineteen forties. 刘天华 Liu Tianhua, eighteen ninety-five to nineteen thirty-two, turned the erhu into a concert solo instrument. Blind street musician 阿炳 Abing, eighteen ninety-three to nineteen fifty: 二泉映月, recorded in nineteen fifty. 聂耳 Nie Er’s 义勇军进行曲 March of the Volunteers, nineteen thirty-five, became the national anthem of the PRC; 冼星海 Xian Xinghai’s 黄河大合唱 Yellow River Cantata, nineteen thirty-nine, rallied people during the War of Resistance.
music/music-history.ac62a5ffe11e: Don't mix up: 义勇军进行曲 was written for a nineteen thirty-five film, years before it became the anthem.
music/music-history.d5099faf0587: Don't mix up: “Classical music,” any orchestral music, versus the Classical period, seventeen fifty to eighteen twenty.

music/music-instruments.194a6da5b4a9: Tanggu and gong 堂鼓, 锣
music/music-instruments.ed6c4665c226: Players pluck with fingernails; the fast “wheel” tremolo 轮指 sounds like a shimmer.
music/music-instruments.5144647bdc31: Timpani. Percussion, tuned drums. A pedal stretches the drumhead tighter to raise the pitch. Usually two to five drums per player. Tighter head, faster vibration, higher pitch, just like the string lab!
music/music-instruments.38f87910c8d2: US standards: Georgia Standards of Excellence, Middle School General Music — M S G M six to eight dot R E dot one, aurally distinguish ensembles, voices and instruments; recognize characteristics of diverse genres and cultures, M S G M six to eight dot C N dot one, principles shared by music and other disciplines — here acoustics or physics, M S G M six to eight dot C N dot two, compare music of world cultures, its functions, musicians and performance conditions.
music/music-instruments.0b640f3b0483: Tanggu and gong 堂鼓, 锣. Percussion, the energy of festivals and opera. 堂鼓: a barrel drum played with two sticks. The gong 锣 and cymbals 镲 add crashes; in Peking opera the percussion section leads the whole show. Drum and gong patterns are called 锣鼓经.
music/music-instruments.38c56e9b291e: The real thing. A tanggu, 堂鼓, barrel drum, Metropolitan Museum of Art.
music/music-instruments.74674c0a48cf: Tuned to the pentatonic scale, 宫商角徵羽, so sweeping glissandos always sound good.
music/music-instruments.cc2edc288172: China: Compulsory Education Arts Curriculum Standards, twenty twenty-two, Music, Stage four, Grades seven to nine — in appreciation, recognizing common Chinese and foreign instruments and their timbres, and the make-up of the Chinese national orchestra, the “cultural understanding” core competency. Also links to Grade eight physics “sound phenomena”, pitch, loudness, timbre; frequency and vibration.
music/music-instruments.6393dc2da82f: The real thing. A pipa, pear-shaped lute, in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
music/music-instruments.a61804827ef2: Bone flutes found at Jiahu, 贾湖, Henan, are about eight thousand to nine thousand years old.
music/music-instruments.29ca3b91efde: Violin. Strings, the orchestra’s melody voice. Four strings tuned G, D, A, E, each a fifth apart. The bow is horsehair rubbed with rosin so it grips the string. A full orchestra has about thirty violins, in “first” and “second” groups.
music/music-instruments.a625de418c1c: Dizi 笛子. Winds, bamboo flute. A bamboo transverse flute with six finger holes. Its secret: an extra hole covered with a thin membrane 笛膜 that buzzes — the bright, reedy sound. Bone flutes found at Jiahu, 贾湖, Henan, are about eight thousand to nine thousand years old.
music/music-instruments.191a6958ea43: Sheng 笙. Winds, mouth organ with free reeds. A bundle of bamboo pipes, each with a small metal reed. It can play chords — rare for a wind instrument. It is about three thousand years old. It appears in the 诗经 Book of Songs. The free-reed idea later inspired the harmonica and the accordion.
music/music-instruments.36d1993e16ad: Memory hint: Bai Juyi’s poem 琵琶行: “big pearls, small pearls, falling on a jade plate” — that is the pipa’s sound.
music/music-instruments.6323e44cc83b: Usually twenty-one strings, each with its own movable bridge.
music/music-instruments.e0edd9cb1997: It has been in China for about two thousand years.
music/music-instruments.37ddd9f5ffa1: Don't mix up: Violin versus erhu: the violin has four strings and a fingerboard; the erhu has two strings and no fingerboard.
music/music-instruments.97a14f59f4e3: National treasure: the bells of Marquis Yi of Zeng, about four hundred thirty-three B C E
music/music-instruments.cf9777a96751: Data: standard tunings, computed in equal temperament with A four equals four hundred forty hertz.
music/music-instruments.ab1bea62e17f: Guzheng 古筝. Plucked strings, zither with moving bridges. Usually twenty-one strings, each with its own movable bridge. Tuned to the pentatonic scale, 宫商角徵羽, so sweeping glissandos always sound good. Pressing the string left of the bridge bends the pitch up — that adds the “missing” notes. Its ancestor, the 秦筝, is more than two thousand years old.
music/music-instruments.e8909ee706d8: Memory hint: 锣鼓喧天 equals drums and gongs fill the sky.
music/music-instruments.9002ae5d3411: Famous piece: “十面埋伏” “Ambush from Ten Sides” — a whole battle told on one instrument.
music/music-instruments.e071b6ee7eca: National Core Arts Standards: M U colon R E seven dot two, M U colon C N one one dot zero. Also connects to Georgia Grade eight Physical Science S eight P four, waves.
music/music-instruments.d6de9991f3e3: Its secret: an extra hole covered with a thin membrane 笛膜 that buzzes — the bright, reedy sound.
music/music-instruments.101fef907dc5: 堂鼓: a barrel drum played with two sticks.
music/music-instruments.3071c9065085: Its ancestor, the 秦筝, is more than two thousand years old.
music/music-instruments.69b697493017: A string’s frequency is: f equals one divided by the quantity two L, times the square root of the quantity T divided by mu. L equals length, T equals tension, mu equals mass per metre. Move the sliders, pluck, and tune to the target note, within plus or minus ten cents. Then lightly touch the string at one half or one third — those are harmonics.
music/music-instruments.fb8bf1a6f65c: Memory hint: 笛膜 equals the dizi’s buzz.
music/music-instruments.96c740369f3b: Memory hint: 笙 equals bamboo bundle that plays chords.
music/music-instruments.3ea955c9f7dc: Memory hint: Guzheng equals twenty-one strings and pentatonic.
music/music-instruments.74a4a7c0af33: A Western orchestra has four families: strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion. A Chinese orchestra has four sections too: bowed strings, plucked strings, winds and percussion. Click an instrument to hear it and read its story. Explore eight or more for stars.
music/music-instruments.a6de69fae9af: Your mission: tune a virtual string to target notes and find its harmonics; walk through a Western orchestra and a Chinese orchestra and ring the two-thousand-four-hundred-year-old bells of Marquis Yi; then become a timbre detective who names instruments by ear alone.

music/music-instruments.a2c193b3fd5f: Notes: the string formula is the ideal-string model; the three linear densities are approximate. Synthesized timbres are approximations. Marquis Yi bell facts, excavated nineteen seventy-eight, sixty-five bells, about four hundred thirty-three B C E, over two thousand five hundred kilograms total, two tones per bell, follow published Hubei Provincial Museum information; the bell pitches on this page are illustrative only.
music/music-instruments.3d832ce07a8d: The real thing. Playing the erhu: the bow sits between the two strings; the left hand presses the strings in mid-air.
music/music-instruments.44bf8f85bfd3: A full orchestra has about thirty violins, in “first” and “second” groups.
music/music-instruments.12edd752609d: Don't mix up: Dizi is played sideways; the 箫 xiao is played straight down.
music/music-instruments.c5a34de95c92: The real thing. The wind section of a Chinese orchestra: dizi players on the left, with a sheng next to them.
music/music-instruments.ea206ee54d98: Erhu 二胡. Bowed strings, the “Chinese violin”. Just two strings, tuned D four and A four — a fifth apart. The bow hair runs BETWEEN the two strings. No fingerboard: fingers press the strings in mid-air, so slides and wide vibrato are easy. Famous piece: 二泉映月, “The Moon Reflected in Erquan Spring” by the blind street musician 阿炳 Abing, eighteen ninety-three to nineteen fifty.
music/music-instruments.c450ab425131: French horn. Brass, mellow and round. About three point seven meters, twelve feet, of tubing wound into a circle. The player puts a hand inside the bell to shape the sound. Its bell points backward.
music/music-instruments.09d1292e91f7: Don't mix up: Western flute versus 笛子 dizi: the dizi is bamboo and has a buzzing membrane hole.

music/music-instruments.ed4200302abd: A string vibrates as a whole AND in two, three, four… parts at once, at two times, three times, four times the basic frequency. The mix of these harmonics is what makes each instrument’s timbre.
music/music-instruments.a189c0f18db7: A violin and an erhu play the same note — A four, four hundred forty vibrations a second — yet you can tell them apart instantly. Why? The secret is in the harmonics: every instrument has its own sound fingerprint, called timbre.
music/music-instruments.fd42262954da: The real thing. A sheng, 笙, mouth organ: a bundle of bamboo pipes, Metropolitan Museum of Art.
music/music-instruments.a968017f5c46: The real thing. Guzheng players of the Yulin Guzheng Band on stage.
music/music-instruments.e94beb19c7d4: Flute. Woodwind, edge-blown. You blow across a hole, like blowing over a bottle — no reed. Range about C four to C seven. It is a woodwind even though it is made of metal.
music/music-instruments.2015d3fd1707: Pipa 琵琶. Plucked strings, pear-shaped lute. Four strings and many frets on a pear-shaped body. Players pluck with fingernails; the fast “wheel” tremolo 轮指 sounds like a shimmer. It has been in China for about two thousand years. Famous piece: 十面埋伏, “Ambush from Ten Sides” — a whole battle told on one instrument.
music/music-instruments.72d629b8ef43: The gong 锣 and cymbals 镲 add crashes; in Peking opera the percussion section leads the whole show.

music/music-instruments.3ff2cddc4679: Just two strings, tuned D four and A four — a fifth apart.

The magic trick: one bell, two notes. Strike the middle of the front or the side and you get two different pitches, about a third apart. Click the middle, 正鼓, or the side, 侧鼓, of each bell and play the opening of “茉莉花” “Jasmine Flower”!
music/music-instruments.d89bd50d5dde: Range about C four to C seven.
music/music-instruments.eac04bb57fa6: Clarinet. Woodwind, single reed. A single cane reed vibrates against the mouthpiece. Its straight, tube-shaped bore makes mostly odd harmonics, one, three, five… — that is its hollow sound. Our synthesizer copies this with a square wave, which has only odd harmonics.

music/music-listening.3e633b184525: Beethoven, Symphony Number five, movement one, Allegro con brio. A motif is a small musical idea a composer can repeat and change. Beethoven starts with three short sounds and a long one. Tap short, short, short, long. Can you still find that pattern when the pitches change?

music/music-pitch.4af44997d30a: Octave. Double the frequency. Go up twelve half steps, eight letter names, and the frequency doubles: A four, four hundred forty hertz. A five, eight hundred eighty hertz. That is why notes repeat their names every octave.
