Seventeen ninety census: about two hundred thirty-eight thousand people; two thousand seven hundred sixty-four were enslaved. Its delegates Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth proposed the Great, Connecticut, Compromise.
ushistory/us-constitution.3304ee1e89a8: Rhode Island. Three of ninety-one votes, Great Compromise. Seventeen ninety census: about sixty-nine thousand people; nine hundred forty-eight were enslaved. The smallest state sent no delegates to the Convention and was the last to ratify — by just two votes.
ushistory/us-constitution.80a898148359: Maryland. Lord Baltimore founded it in sixteen thirty-four as a refuge for Catholics, and its Toleration Act of sixteen forty-nine protected Christians of different churches. In the Civil War it was a slave state that stayed in the Union, and Lee’s first invasion of the North was stopped here at Antietam.
ushistory/us-constitution.01b5117b1200: North Carolina. Ratified November twenty-first, seventeen eighty-nine, vote one hundred ninety-four to seventy-seven, number twelve. Seventeen ninety census: about three hundred ninety-four thousand people; about one hundred one thousand were enslaved. Refused to ratify at first, seventeen eighty-eight, and waited until a bill of rights was on the way; joined in November seventeen eighty-nine.
ushistory/us-constitution.1ee7336f931d: Rhode Island. Roger Williams founded it in sixteen thirty-six as a place where the government could not force anyone’s religion. It was so independent that it skipped the Constitutional Convention and ratified last, by just thirty-four votes to thirty-two, in seventeen ninety.
ushistory/us-constitution.08f3ed23896f: Maryland. Seven of ninety-one votes, Great Compromise. Seventeen ninety census: about three hundred twenty thousand people; about one hundred three thousand were enslaved. Its delegate Luther Martin walked out of the Convention and fought ratification — but Maryland voted yes, sixty-three to eleven.
ushistory/us-constitution.52a01df498dc: South Carolina. Ratified May twenty-third, seventeen eighty-eight, vote one hundred forty-nine to seventy-three, number eight. Seventeen ninety census: about two hundred forty-nine thousand people; about one hundred seven thousand were enslaved. Its delegates pushed hard to count enslaved people and to protect the slave trade.
ushistory/us-constitution.f79efc9c03a1: North Carolina. Nine of ninety-one votes, Great Compromise. Seventeen ninety census: about three hundred ninety-four thousand people; about one hundred one thousand were enslaved. Refused to ratify at first, seventeen eighty-eight, and waited until a bill of rights was on the way; joined in November seventeen eighty-nine.
ushistory/us-constitution.8762464e403f: New Hampshire. Five of ninety-one votes, Great Compromise. Seventeen ninety census: about one hundred forty-two thousand people; one hundred fifty-eight were enslaved. The ninth “yes” — with this vote the Constitution went into effect.
ushistory/us-constitution.f5ab6f5d1000: New Hampshire. Its giant white pines were so valuable that the king’s men marked the best ones as masts for the Royal Navy. On the twenty-first of June, seventeen eighty-eight, it became the ninth state to approve the Constitution — exactly the number needed for it to take effect.
ushistory/us-constitution.3bbc62bc2243: Delaware. Swedes, then the Dutch, then the English ruled it. On the seventh of December, seventeen eighty-seven, it became the first state to ratify the Constitution — every vote was yes — so it calls itself “The First State”; in the Civil War it was a slave state that stayed in the Union.
ushistory/us-constitution.23cd4b245ed2: Virginia. Ratified June twenty-fifth, seventeen eighty-eight, vote eighty-nine to seventy-nine, number ten. Seventeen ninety census: about seven hundred forty-eight thousand people; about two hundred ninety-three thousand were enslaved. The biggest state. James Madison’s Virginia Plan gave big states more votes. Patrick Henry led the Anti-Federalists here.
ushistory/us-constitution.c4cae33f0740: New Jersey. Five of ninety-one votes, Great Compromise. Seventeen ninety census: about one hundred eighty-four thousand people; about eleven thousand were enslaved. William Paterson’s New Jersey Plan: one vote per state, just like the Articles.

ushistory/us-expansion.1782adcdb3e3: The Louisiana Purchase. Bought from France, eighteen oh three. Fifteen million dollars — about three cents an acre. President Thomas Jefferson only wanted the port of New Orleans. Napoleon, short of money for his wars in Europe, offered the whole territory. It roughly doubled the size of the country — about eight hundred twenty-eight thousand square miles, parts of fifteen future states. Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, the Corps of Discovery, to explore it, eighteen oh four to eighteen oh six.
ushistory/us-expansion.c88778c44a2b: Texas Annexation. Annexed, eighteen forty-five, independent Republic of Texas eighteen thirty-six to eighteen forty-five. Joined by vote of Congress; Mexico did not accept it. American settlers, invited by Mexico in the eighteen twenties, outnumbered Tejanos, Mexican Texans, by the eighteen thirties. Many brought enslaved people, although Mexico had abolished slavery in eighteen twenty-nine. Texas won independence in eighteen thirty-six, the Alamo, then victory at San Jacinto. Annexation in eighteen forty-five led straight to war with Mexico, because both countries claimed the land between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande.
ushistory/us-expansion.78ba4f396d6e: The Mexican Cession. From Mexico, Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, eighteen forty-eight, after the Mexican-American War. Fifteen million dollars, plus up to three point two five million dollars in claims. The Mexican-American War, eighteen forty-six to eighteen forty-eight, ended with US troops in Mexico City. Mexico lost about half of its territory — today’s California, Nevada, Utah and parts of four more states. About eighty thousand to one hundred thousand Mexican citizens living there could become US citizens; many later lost their land in courts.
ushistory/us-expansion.8cb8cfd9a9d6: The United States in seventeen eighty-three. From Britain, Treaty of Paris, seventeen eighty-three. Won in the Revolutionary War. The Treaty of Paris ended the American Revolution. Britain recognised US independence. The new border ran west to the Mississippi River, north to the Great Lakes, and south to Spanish Florida. Land between the Appalachians and the Mississippi was home to many Native nations — Shawnee, Miami, Cherokee, Creek and others — who had not signed the treaty.
ushistory/us-expansion.1ea3b4124144: Don't mix up: The thirteen states were only the eastern strip; the land out to the Mississippi was organised into territories later, for example the Northwest Territory, seventeen eighty-seven.
ushistory/us-expansion.3b277e5d7643: Don't mix up: Florida was Spanish, then British, seventeen sixty-three to seventeen eighty-three, then Spanish again before eighteen nineteen.
ushistory/us-expansion.2ba75f0deb23: Florida. From Spain, Adams-Onís Treaty, eighteen nineteen. US paid five million dollars of its citizens’ claims against Spain. After raids across the border and General Andrew Jackson’s invasion in eighteen eighteen, Spain agreed to give up Florida. The treaty also drew the border between the US and Spanish Mexico all the way to the Pacific. Seminole people in Florida later fought removal for decades.
ushistory/us-expansion.d401490ed982: The Gadsden Purchase. Bought from Mexico, eighteen fifty-three. Ten million dollars. The US wanted flat land south of the Gila River for a southern railroad to California. It completed the borders of the “lower forty-eight” states. Next came Alaska, bought from Russia, eighteen sixty-seven, and Hawaii, annexed eighteen ninety-eight.
ushistory/us-expansion.9d665882a61f: Red River Basin. From Britain, Convention of eighteen eighteen. Treaty — no payment. The US and Britain agreed that the border would run along the forty-ninth parallel, forty-nine degrees north, from Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains. The two countries also agreed to share the Oregon Country for the time being.
ushistory/us-expansion.8b53534e7fcb: Oregon Country. From Britain, Oregon Treaty, eighteen forty-six. Treaty — split at forty-nine degrees north, no payment. From eighteen eighteen the US and Britain shared the Oregon Country. Thousands of American settlers arrived on the Oregon Trail from eighteen forty-three. Some Americans shouted “Fifty-four forty or fight!”, fifty-four degrees forty minutes north, but President Polk compromised at forty-nine degrees north. The Chinook, Nez Perce, Cayuse and many other nations had lived here for thousands of years.
ushistory/us-expansion.039869edf91a: Don't mix up: Texas was annexed, not bought. Its old claims stretched north to today’s Wyoming; it gave them up in eighteen fifty.

ushistory/us-industrial.4c6e4fddb136: Boston, Massachusetts. Telephone, eighteen seventy-six. Bell, a teacher of deaf students, patented the telephone in March eighteen seventy-six. First words: “Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.” By nineteen hundred there were well over a million telephones in the US.
ushistory/us-industrial.aa3564de0142: Angel Island, San Francisco Bay. Open nineteen ten to nineteen forty. Many arrivals came from China and Japan. Because of the Chinese Exclusion Act, 排华法案, eighteen eighty-two, Chinese immigrants were often held for weeks or months and questioned closely. Detainees carved poems in Chinese into the wooden walls — you can still read them today. The law was not repealed until nineteen forty-three, when China was a US ally in World War Two.
ushistory/us-industrial.b3e862f62942: Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The seventeenth of December, nineteen oh three. Orville and Wilbur Wright, bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, chose the windy sand dunes at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk. First flight: twelve seconds, one hundred twenty feet — shorter than a Boeing seven four seven’s wingspan. The best flight that day lasted fifty-nine seconds, eight hundred fifty-two feet. They tested wings in a home-made wind tunnel first.
ushistory/us-industrial.2fc8f7d7a92a: Promontory Summit, Utah. The tenth of May, eighteen sixty-nine. The telegraph flashed one word across the nation when the last spike went in: “DONE.” Central Pacific workers had laid ten miles of track in a single day a few days earlier — a record.
ushistory/us-industrial.98f5cc34c025: Ellis Island, New York Harbor. Open eighteen ninety-two to nineteen fifty-four. Before eighteen ninety-two, New York’s immigrants came through Castle Garden, eighteen fifty-five to eighteen ninety, at the tip of Manhattan. Most came from Europe — Italy, Austria-Hungary, the Russian Empire, Ireland, Germany. Record day: eleven thousand seven hundred forty-seven people on the seventeenth of April, nineteen oh seven. Ships’ first- and second-class passengers were usually checked on board; steerage, third-class, passengers took a ferry to the island.
ushistory/us-industrial.bc420c71b3be: Don't mix up: Telegraph, eighteen forty-four, equals dots and dashes; telephone, eighteen seventy-six, equals voices.
ushistory/us-industrial.1127e724761f: Don't mix up: Ellis Island is next to the Statue of Liberty, eighteen eighty-six, but they are different islands.
ushistory/us-industrial.2d7b89a96ced: Detroit, Michigan. Model T nineteen oh eight, moving assembly line nineteen thirteen. Henry Ford’s Model T, nineteen oh eight, was built to be simple, tough and cheap. In nineteen thirteen Ford’s Highland Park plant added a moving assembly line, 流水线: building a chassis dropped from about twelve and a half hours to about one and a half hours. The price fell from eight hundred fifty dollars, nineteen oh eight, to under four hundred dollars by nineteen sixteen — ordinary families could buy a car.
ushistory/us-industrial.cc9f4b39fd4b: The first transcontinental railroad. Golden spike: the tenth of May, eighteen sixty-nine. Union Pacific built west from Omaha; Central Pacific built east from Sacramento. They met at Promontory Summit, Utah. The Central Pacific hired thousands of Chinese workers, 华工 — at the peak most of its workforce. They blasted tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada. A coast-to-coast trip shrank from months to about a week.
ushistory/us-industrial.65fd52dd6473: Don't mix up: Angel Island opened in nineteen ten — after the Exclusion Act, so its job was often to keep people out.
ushistory/us-industrial.22051689a4c9: Memory hook: “sixty-nine — the spike is fine”: East meets West in Utah.
ushistory/us-industrial.362f87cb160d: Tuskegee Institute, Alabama. Carver arrives eighteen ninety-six. Born enslaved in Missouri, Carver became a scientist and teacher at Tuskegee. Growing only cotton wore out Southern soil. He taught farmers crop rotation, 轮作, with peanuts and sweet potatoes, which put nitrogen back in the soil. He found hundreds of uses for peanuts, sweet potatoes and other crops to give farmers new markets.
ushistory/us-industrial.7d727d83d8f4: Memory hook: Bell rang in eighteen seventy-six — the nation’s hundredth birthday.
ushistory/us-industrial.00c32f2e6d72: Memory hook: Edison: sound in seventy-seven, light in seventy-nine.
ushistory/us-industrial.1698bf44aba2: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Steel city from eighteen seventy-five. Andrew Carnegie opened his Edgar Thomson Steel Works near Pittsburgh in eighteen seventy-five, using the Bessemer process, 贝塞麦炼钢法, to make cheap steel. Coal from nearby hills and three rivers for shipping made it the perfect spot. Steel went into rails, bridges and skyscrapers. Thousands of immigrants from Eastern Europe worked in the mills.
ushistory/us-industrial.31a7568022a2: Chicago, Illinois. Union Stock Yards open eighteen sixty-five. More railroads met in Chicago than anywhere else in America. Cattle and hogs arrived by train; meatpackers like Swift used refrigerated rail cars, about eighteen eighty, to ship fresh meat east. Population: about thirty thousand in eighteen fifty, about one point seven million in nineteen hundred.
ushistory/us-industrial.f54da36c49f4: Memory hook: nineteen oh three: twelve seconds that changed travel.
ushistory/us-industrial.1778d4d4d2f3: New York to Chicago lines. Through to Chicago by the early eighteen fifties. Several railroads linked end to end, following the old Erie Canal route across New York. Chicago became the place where eastern and western lines met — the hub of the nation.
ushistory/us-industrial.7861b44d9e03: Menlo Park, New Jersey. Edison’s lab, eighteen seventy-six. Thomas Edison built a lab where a team invented things on purpose, every day. Phonograph eighteen seventy-seven; a long-lasting light bulb eighteen seventy-nine. In eighteen eighty-two his Pearl Street station began selling electric power in New York City. He held more than one thousand US patents, 专利.
ushistory/us-industrial.4c332f886d34: Southern lines through Atlanta. Charleston to Atlanta to Memphis by eighteen fifty-seven. Atlanta was founded as a railroad end point, it was first called “Terminus”. The South had far fewer miles of track than the North — a big problem in the Civil War.
ushistory/us-industrial.db6bd43e6a9a: Memory hook: sixty-nine — the spike is fine.
ushistory/us-industrial.179d65cc3723: Memory hook: eighteen eighty-two shut the door; nineteen forty-three opened it a crack.
ushistory/us-industrial.b609034810d0: The Chisholm Trail. Used about eighteen sixty-seven to eighteen eighty-four. After the Civil War, a longhorn steer worth about four dollars in Texas could sell for around forty dollars in the North — a price incentive, 价格刺激, that drove the trail. Cowboys drove herds of a few thousand cattle about ten to twelve miles a day for weeks, to railheads like Abilene, Kansas. Millions of cattle went up the trails. Many cowboys were Black or Mexican American. Barbed wire and new rail lines into Texas ended the long drives by the late eighteen eighties.

ushistory/us-modern.104545937a4a: Houston: Mission Control. Nineteen sixty-five to today, Texas. NASA’s Manned Spacecraft Center, now the Johnson Space Center, took over Mission Control for crewed flights starting with Gemini four in nineteen sixty-five. July twentieth, nineteen sixty-nine: “Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.” Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between nineteen sixty-nine and nineteen seventy-two — all of them American.
ushistory/us-modern.da8348a10ede: Don’t mix up: Yuri Gagarin, USSR, April nineteen sixty-one, was the first human in space; Alan Shepard, May nineteen sixty-one, was the first American.
ushistory/us-modern.266bc51e30ef: Don’t mix up: NATO, nineteen forty-nine, was the US and Western Europe’s alliance; the Warsaw Pact, nineteen fifty-five, was the Soviet side’s alliance.
ushistory/us-modern.177d47120537: Don’t mix up: Microsoft was founded in nineteen seventy-five in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and moved to Washington State — not Silicon Valley.
ushistory/us-modern.76509e4e2e04: Washington: containment and NATO. Nineteen forty-seven, nineteen forty-nine, nineteen fifty-eight. Nineteen forty-seven: the Truman Doctrine promised help to countries resisting communism — a policy called containment, 遏制. April fourth, nineteen forty-nine: twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, creating NATO, 北约: “an attack on one is an attack on all.” Nineteen fifty-eight: after Sputnik, Congress created NASA. After the Cuban crisis, a Washington-Moscow “hotline”, nineteen sixty-three, let leaders talk directly.
ushistory/us-modern.78ce052cf7bb: Huntsville, Alabama: “Rocket City”. Marshall Space Flight Center, nineteen sixty. Wernher von Braun’s rocket team at the Redstone Arsenal built the rocket that launched Explorer one. NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center opened here in nineteen sixty and developed the Saturn five Moon rocket. The Saturn five stood three hundred sixty-three feet, one hundred eleven meters, tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty with its pedestal. Today Huntsville hosts Space Camp.
ushistory/us-modern.14d8bc8b9ecf: Cuban Missile Crisis. October sixteenth to twenty-eighth, nineteen sixty-two. After its nineteen fifty-nine revolution, Cuba under Fidel Castro allied with the Soviet Union. A US U two spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites about ninety miles, one hundred forty-five kilometers, from Florida. For thirteen days the world held its breath. Kennedy ordered a naval “quarantine”. Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles; the US promised not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey.
ushistory/us-modern.af0a2a419dea: Silicon Valley, California. Nineteen seventy-one to today. Named after the silicon used to make computer chips. In nineteen seventy-one Intel released the first commercial microprocessor — a computer’s “brain” on one chip. Nineteen seventy-six: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak founded Apple; the Apple two, nineteen seventy-seven, was one of the first popular home computers. IBM’s PC followed in nineteen eighty-one. Nineteen ninety-eight: Google was founded. Two thousand seven: Apple’s iPhone put the internet in people’s pockets.
ushistory/us-modern.27b6dcaa4100: ARPANET: the first four nodes. October twenty-ninth, nineteen sixty-nine, California and Utah. ARPA, a Defense Department agency set up in nineteen fifty-eight after Sputnik, paid for a network linking university computers. The first message went from UCLA to SRI: they tried to type “LOGIN”, but the system crashed after “L O”. By December four sites were linked. It used packet switching: messages are chopped into small packets that each find their own way. In nineteen eighty-three ARPANET switched to T C P I P — the common language of today’s internet.
ushistory/us-modern.8b1d9e660b9c: Don’t mix up: The failed Bay of Pigs invasion was in nineteen sixty-one; the Missile Crisis was in nineteen sixty-two, and the US did not invade.
ushistory/us-modern.5949e5655f42: Cape Canaveral and Kennedy Space Center. Nineteen fifty-eight to today, Florida. January thirty-first, nineteen fifty-eight: Explorer one, the first US satellite, launched here and discovered radiation belts around Earth. May fifth, nineteen sixty-one: Alan Shepard became the first American in space. February twentieth, nineteen sixty-two: John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth, three orbits. July sixteenth, nineteen sixty-nine: Apollo eleven lifted off on a Saturn five rocket. Why Florida? It is far south, and rockets fly out over the ocean.
ushistory/us-modern.9cdf212f5a30: Don’t mix up: Apollo eleven launched from Florida; Houston was Mission Control.
ushistory/us-modern.7d702c2f7fa5: Trinity test, New Mexico. July sixteenth, nineteen forty-five. Scientists of the secret Manhattan Project, based at Los Alamos, tested the first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. In August nineteen forty-five the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrendered and World War two ended. In nineteen forty-nine the Soviet Union tested its own bomb. The nuclear arms race, 军备竞赛, had begun.
ushistory/us-modern.8600395b06e5: September eleventh, two thousand one. New York, Arlington, Virginia, Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Terrorists of the al-Qaeda group hijacked four passenger planes. Two struck the World Trade Center in New York and one struck the Pentagon. Passengers on United Flight ninety-three fought back; the plane crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Nearly three thousand people died that day. Afterwards the US created the Department of Homeland Security, tightened airport security and went to war in Afghanistan. Memorials stand at all three sites.

ushistory/us-worldwars.1eace61f10bf: Manzanar, California. Executive Order nine zero six six, nineteen forty-two. After Pearl Harbor, fear and prejudice led FDR to sign Executive Order nine zero six six, nineteen forty-two. About one hundred twenty thousand people of Japanese ancestry — two-thirds of them US citizens — were sent to camps such as Manzanar. No Japanese American was ever convicted of spying. Many young Japanese American men still served; the four hundred forty-second Regiment became one of the most decorated units. In nineteen eighty-eight the US government formally apologized and paid survivors.
ushistory/us-worldwars.a18458b4da93: The Great Migration. About nineteen fifteen to nineteen seventy. Push: Jim Crow segregation laws, 种族隔离法, violence, and poor pay as sharecroppers in the South. Pull: factory jobs in Chicago, Detroit, New York, Philadelphia — first in World War one, again in World War two. Black newspapers like the Chicago Defender urged people to come. In the second wave, nineteen forty to nineteen seventy, many went west too: Los Angeles, Oakland and the Bay Area shipyards. It reshaped American cities, music, jazz, blues, and politics — and fed the Harlem Renaissance.

worldhistory/wh-cold-war.052adeaf62dc: The Soviet Union breaks up. December nineteen ninety-one. The Warsaw Pact dissolved in July nineteen ninety-one. In December the USSR split into fifteen independent countries, and Gorbachev resigned. The Cold War’s two-pole world was over. China’s textbook describes a world moving toward many centres of power, 多极化.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.92b0ccb80e5b: Don’t mix up: Russia is the largest of the fifteen countries that came out of the USSR — not the same thing as the USSR.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.04af5cc1ca25: Independence for India and Pakistan. August fifteenth, nineteen forty-seven. Mohandas Gandhi led mass non-violent protests against British rule, such as the nineteen thirty Salt March. Britain left in nineteen forty-seven; British India was split, partitioned, into India and Pakistan. Millions were forced to move and many died in violence. India’s independence encouraged freedom movements across Asia and Africa.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.52c9715bf48f: Don’t mix up: Bangladesh, once East Pakistan, became independent later, in nineteen seventy-one.

worldhistory/wh-exploration.d1f6a1856fb0: The Manila galleons, Spain. Fifteen sixty-five to eighteen fifteen. American silver across the Pacific to buy Chinese silk and porcelain. Each year Spanish galleons sailed between Acapulco, Mexico, and Manila, Philippines. They carried silver mined in Mexico and Peru; Chinese merchants in Manila traded silk and porcelain for it. A huge share of the world’s silver flowed to Ming China — and the Ming began collecting taxes in silver.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.94104098ef76: Bartolomeu Dias, Portugal. Fourteen eighty-seven to fourteen eighty-eight. First European to sail round the southern tip of Africa. Portugal had crept down Africa’s coast for seventy years, looking for gold and a sea road to Asian spices. A storm blew Dias’s two caravels far south; turning east, then north, he found the coast running east — Africa had an end! His tired crew made him turn back. The king renamed the “Cape of Storms” the Cape of Good Hope.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.7ce79204e124: Zheng He, China, Ming. Seven voyages, fourteen oh five to fourteen thirty-three. “Down to the Western Oceans” with the biggest wooden fleet of its time. The first voyage: sixty-two large “treasure ships” and over twenty-seven thousand eight hundred men, Ming History; two hundred or more ships in all are often quoted. Over twenty-eight years the fleet visited thirty or more countries and regions of Asia and Africa — as far as the east coast of Africa and the Red Sea. It carried silk and porcelain and brought back spices, gems — and a giraffe for the emperor, fourteen fourteen. Goal: show the Ming emperor’s power and build friendly “tribute” ties — not conquest or colonies. The voyages stopped after fourteen thirty-three.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.dac36cd05fb8: Magellan and Elcano, sailing for Spain. Fifteen nineteen to fifteen twenty-two. The first voyage all the way around the world. Five ships and about two hundred seventy men left Spain in fifteen nineteen to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. They found a stormy passage at South America’s tip, the Strait of Magellan, and entered an ocean so calm Magellan called it the “Pacific”. The crossing took about ninety-eight days; the crew ate leather and sawdust, and scurvy killed many. Magellan was killed in fifteen twenty-one in a battle on Mactan in the Philippines. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship, the Victoria, home with eighteen men in fifteen twenty-two.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.0c04e35a8ce6: The Atlantic “triangle trade”. Fifteen hundreds to eighteen sixties. Goods, Africa; enslaved people, Americas; sugar, cotton, silver, Europe. Outward: European ships carried cloth, guns and metal goods to West Africa. Middle passage: about twelve point five million Africans were forced onto slave ships; about ten point seven million survived the crossing, Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. Homeward: sugar, tobacco, cotton and silver made in the Americas went back to Europe. Africa lost millions of young people; enslaved people and their descendants built much of the Americas’ wealth.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.5881b12dda41: Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain. Fourteen ninety-two to fourteen ninety-three. Sailed west to reach Asia — and reached the Americas. An Italian from Genoa, paid by Spain’s Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand. Three ships: Niña, Pinta and Santa María. He believed Earth was round, true, but much smaller than it is, false — he thought Japan was about where America is. October twelfth, fourteen ninety-two: landing in the Bahamas, home of the Taíno people. He called them “Indians” because he thought he was in the Indies. His voyages began Spanish conquest and colonies; Taíno numbers collapsed from disease, forced labour and violence.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.fb7331d8aa4b: Vasco da Gama, Portugal. Fourteen ninety-seven to fourteen ninety-nine, India: May fourteen ninety-eight. Opened the sea road from Europe to India. Four ships, about one hundred seventy men. In the South Atlantic he swung far out to sea — about three months without seeing land. In East Africa, Malindi, he took on a local pilot who knew the monsoon winds across the Indian Ocean. He reached Calicut, India, in May fourteen ninety-eight. Only about fifty-five of his men made it home — many died of scurvy. The pepper and spices he brought back paid for the voyage many times over.

worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.09000579ded7: Egypt: New Kingdom. Circa fifteen fifty to ten sixty-nine B C E, peak under Thutmose the third, circa fourteen fifty B C E. Under Thutmose the third, fifteenth century B C E, Egypt became a great empire spanning Africa and Asia, from Nubia to the Euphrates. Pharaohs were now buried in the Valley of the Kings near Thebes — including Tutankhamun, circa thirteen twenty-three B C E.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.3b5dc1971a69: Persian, Achaemenid, Empire. Five hundred fifty to three hundred thirty B C E. Cyrus the Great built an empire from Anatolia, Turkey, to Central Asia. It took Babylon in five hundred thirty-nine B C E. Next lesson: how the Persians ran such a huge empire with roads, satraps and coins.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.56b75707369a: Ptolemaic Egypt. Three hundred five to thirty B C E. Alexander the Great took Egypt in three hundred thirty-two B C E and founded Alexandria. His general Ptolemy’s family then ruled as pharaohs. The Rosetta Stone, one hundred ninety-six B C E, is one of their decrees. Cleopatra the seventh was the last; in thirty B C E Egypt became a province of Rome.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.b5c67536e4b8: Akkadian Empire. Circa twenty-three thirty-four to twenty-one fifty-four B C E. Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian cities and created what is often called the first empire: many peoples under one ruler. It lasted less than two hundred years before breaking apart.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.adfaffe77e74: Egypt: Early Dynastic and Old Kingdom. Circa thirty-one hundred to twenty-one eighty-one B C E. Around thirty-one hundred B C E Upper, southern, and Lower, northern, Egypt were united under one king — traditionally Narmer, Menes. The Old Kingdom is the “Age of the Pyramids”: Djoser’s step pyramid, circa twenty-six fifty B C E, and the Great Pyramid of Khufu, circa twenty-five sixty B C E. The pharaoh was seen as a living god with absolute power.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.a5c621f5e002: Neo-Babylonian, Chaldean, Empire. Circa six hundred twenty-six to five hundred thirty-nine B C E. King Nebuchadnezzar the second rebuilt Babylon with the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate. Stories of the “Hanging Gardens” come from this time, no one has found them. In five hundred thirty-nine B C E Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon without a long siege.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.2163ab511b2c: Assyrian Empire. Empire circa seven hundred forty-five to six hundred nine B C E. At its largest, circa six hundred seventy B C E, Assyria ruled from Egypt to western Iran — the biggest empire the world had yet seen. King Ashurbanipal collected a library of thousands of clay tablets at Nineveh, including the Epic of Gilgamesh.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.0f0d31ed2f68: Old Babylonian Kingdom, Hammurabi. Circa eighteen ninety-four to fifteen ninety-five B C E, Hammurabi ruled circa seventeen ninety-two to seventeen fifty B C E. Around the eighteenth century B C E, King Hammurabi united most of Mesopotamia under Babylon. He issued the Code of Hammurabi — two hundred eighty-two laws carved on a stone pillar, the oldest fairly complete written law code to survive. It showed that the king’s power came from the gods.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.191fd3490081: Third Dynasty of Ur. Circa twenty-one twelve to two thousand four B C E. King Ur-Nammu built the great Ziggurat of Ur and issued the Code of Ur-Nammu — the oldest law code that survives, in fragments. Scribes kept records of almost everything: sheep, grain, workers’ wages.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.af1d134de15f: Empire of Alexander the Great. Three hundred thirty-four to three hundred twenty-three B C E, then fought over by his generals. Alexander of Macedon conquered the whole Persian Empire in about ten years, from Egypt to the Indus. After he died in Babylon in three hundred twenty-three B C E, his generals split the empire.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.996ba444c821: Sumerian city-states. Circa thirty-five hundred to twenty-three thirty-four B C E. Dozens of independent cities — Uruk, Ur, Lagash and more — each with its own king, walls, canals and a temple for its god. Uruk grew to perhaps forty thousand people around three thousand B C E, one of the first true cities. The Sumerians invented cuneiform writing, circa thirty-two hundred B C E, and the wheel.
worldhistory/wh-first-civilizations.f8524ded308b: Persian, Achaemenid, Empire. Persia ruled Egypt from five hundred twenty-five B C E. In five hundred twenty-five B C E King Cambyses the second added Egypt. Now one empire held both Mesopotamia and Egypt — and reached the Indus. Egypt broke free four hundred four to three hundred forty-three B C E before Persia took it back, not shown.

worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.4a9eb887739c: Carthage, near Tunis. A Phoenician trading city in North Africa and Rome’s great rival. Rome fought it in three Punic Wars, two hundred sixty-four to one hundred forty-six B C E, and destroyed it in one hundred forty-six B C E; Romans later rebuilt it as a Roman city.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.aaa160f91465: Syracuse. A rich Greek colony on Sicily, founded by Corinth about seven hundred thirty-three B C E. Home of the mathematician Archimedes, died two hundred twelve B C E.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.df35d2ccf59b: Rome. Legend says Rome was founded in seven hundred fifty-three B C E on seven hills by the Tiber River. Republic from five hundred nine B C E, Empire from twenty-seven B C E; about a million people lived here around one C E, estimate.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.4423f262aec0: Olympia. Site of the ancient Olympic Games, held every four years for Zeus from seven hundred seventy-six B C E. During the games a truce let athletes travel safely.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.63c261ff6f43: Massalia, Marseille. Greek colony founded about six hundred B C E — today Marseille, France. Greeks spread colonies all around the Mediterranean and Black Sea “like frogs around a pond”, Plato.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.92c89aa9e3b1: Coloured areas show who ruled where in the year on the slider. Borders are rough — ancient empires had no exact lines on the ground. Pericles: Leader of Athens in its golden age; paid citizens for public service and built the Parthenon. Socrates, Plato, Aristotle: Three Athenian philosophers: teacher, student, student. Aristotle then taught Alexander. Alexander the Great: King of Macedon, three hundred thirty-six to three hundred twenty-three B C E; conquered from Greece to the Indus River and spread Greek culture. Hannibal: Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps with elephants in two hundred eighteen B C E. Julius Caesar: Conquered Gaul, became dictator, was killed in forty-four B C E. Augustus, Octavian: First Roman emperor, twenty-seven B C E to fourteen C E; began two centuries of “Roman Peace”, Pax Romana.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.720efc743283: Babylon, near Baghdad. Conquered by Cyrus of Persia in five hundred thirty-nine B C E. Alexander died here in three hundred twenty-three B C E, aged thirty-two.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.c32068e28f6b: Hadrian’s Wall. A stone wall about one hundred eighteen kilometers long across northern Britain, guarding the edge of the Roman Empire. Soldiers lived in forts along it.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.3b22d5410803: Athens. The leading sea power of Greece and birthplace of democracy, reforms of Solon five hundred ninety-four B C E and Cleisthenes five hundred eight B C E. Under Pericles, about four hundred sixty-one to four hundred twenty-nine B C E, it built the Parthenon and led the Delian League.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.094a7da8e20b: Sparta. A land power in the Peloponnese whose citizens trained as soldiers from age seven. Led the Peloponnesian League and defeated Athens in four hundred four B C E.

worldhistory/wh-india-persia.8d079bb1f0b4: Mohenjo-daro. today: Sindh, Pakistan. Perhaps forty thousand people — one of the biggest cities in the world four thousand five hundred years ago. Streets laid out in a grid, covered brick drains, hundreds of wells and the “Great Bath”. Its writing, the Indus script, on small stone seals, has never been deciphered.
worldhistory/wh-india-persia.f328ef5a8ccd: Chang’an. today: Xi’an, China. Capital of the Western Han. Zhang Qian set out from here, one hundred thirty-eight B C E — the start of the Silk Road.
worldhistory/wh-india-persia.bef74783f4a4: Sanchi. today: Madhya Pradesh, India. Ashoka began the Great Stupa here, a dome-shaped Buddhist monument holding relics. Its carved stone gateways were added about two thousand years ago.
worldhistory/wh-india-persia.005a8bf72bcc: Harappa. today: Punjab, Pakistan. The first Indus city dug up by archaeologists, nineteen twenties — so the whole culture is also called “Harappan”. Large granaries, brick houses and wells; perhaps twenty-three thousand or more people at its height.
worldhistory/wh-india-persia.c070e39edbfe: Babylon. near Hillah, Iraq. Cyrus took Babylon in five hundred thirty-nine B C E and recorded it on the Cyrus Cylinder. Alexander the Great died here in three hundred twenty-three B C E.
worldhistory/wh-india-persia.2bcfe6287a20: Persepolis. near Shiraz, Iran. Darius the first began this ceremonial capital around five hundred eighteen B C E. Stone reliefs show people from all over the empire bringing gifts to the king. Alexander’s army burned it in three hundred thirty B C E; the ruins still stand.
worldhistory/wh-india-persia.0005b57b3133: Kalinga, Dhauli. today: Odisha, India. Ashoka conquered Kalinga in about two hundred sixty-one B C E. In his own words, the suffering of the war filled him with deep regret. At Dhauli, near the battlefield, his edicts are still carved into a rock.

worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.52bdfd74e64b: Damascus. Capital of the Umayyad caliphs, six hundred sixty-one to seven hundred fifty.
worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.1e22fb9b3fcc: Paris. Capital of the French kings; its university grew around twelve hundred; Notre-Dame was begun in eleven sixty-three.
worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.dcc9a8520b8e: Historians call four hundred seventy-six to fifteen hundred in Europe the Middle Ages, 中世纪 — the “middle” between ancient Rome and the modern world. Memory hook. “Four hundred seventy-six, the West falls. Eight hundred, Charlemagne crowned. Eight hundred forty-three, split in three. Fourteen fifty-three, the East falls.”
worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.254664c10515: Frankish kingdom. Clovis united the Franks and founded the kingdom, four hundred eighty-six; he became a Christian, winning the support of the Church. Most of today’s France and western Germany.
worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.2aee01efa336: Eastern Roman Empire. When the West fell in four hundred seventy-six, the East — rich, with strong walls around Constantinople — survived. Greek-speaking, Christian, and still calling itself “Roman”.
worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.8354c40c9c18: Samarkand. A Silk Road city; paper-making was known here by the seven hundreds.

worldhistory/wh-renaissance.dbdccd718aed: “Renaissance”, 文艺复兴, means “rebirth”: scholars revived Greek and Roman learning — but used it to celebrate human talent and life in this world. That idea is called humanism, 人文主义. Memory hook. “Fourteen fifty, the press. Fifteen seventeen, the protest. Fifteen fifty-five, the split.”
worldhistory/wh-renaissance.2ffd52ead05f: Don’t mix up: The Renaissance, art and ideas, from the thirteen hundreds, and the Reformation, religion, from fifteen seventeen, overlap, but they are different movements. Printing helped both.

worldhistory/wh-today.3c93768b8b6f: Don’t mix up: The SDGs, twenty fifteen to twenty thirty, replaced the earlier Millennium Development Goals, two thousand to twenty fifteen.
worldhistory/wh-today.ffb55f85ff4f: The European Coal and Steel Community. Nineteen fifty-one to nineteen fifty-two. France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg pooled their coal and steel — the materials for weapons. French minister Robert Schuman wanted to make war between France and Germany “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.” It grew into the European Economic Community, nineteen fifty-eight, and the European Union, nineteen ninety-three.
worldhistory/wh-today.74e46e4b9934: The UK leaves the EU. January thirty-first, twenty twenty. In a twenty sixteen vote, fifty-two percent of British voters chose to leave the EU. The UK left in twenty twenty — the first country ever to leave. The EU now has twenty-seven members.
worldhistory/wh-today.e3ae4b38f38f: The World Trade Organization. Nineteen ninety-five, Geneva. The WTO replaced the GATT, nineteen forty-seven. Its members agree on trade rules and settle trade disputes. Over one hundred sixty members cover about ninety-eight percent of world trade.
worldhistory/wh-today.f9c4b3a94f51: The Treaty of Rome: a common market. Nineteen fifty-seven, in force nineteen fifty-eight. The six created the European Economic Community: no tariffs between members and one tariff for goods from outside. Trade among them grew fast; more countries joined in nineteen seventy-three, nineteen eighty-one, nineteen eighty-six and nineteen ninety-five.
worldhistory/wh-today.0a0dc5cf7b6d: Euro coins and notes. January first, two thousand two, currency since nineteen ninety-nine. Twelve countries swapped their old money for euros overnight; the European Central Bank is in Frankfurt. Today more than twenty EU countries use the euro, Bulgaria joined in twenty twenty-six. Some EU members, like Denmark and Sweden, keep their own currency.
worldhistory/wh-today.7c9886905809: One ship blocks world trade. March twenty twenty-one. The giant container ship Ever Given, about four hundred meters, one thousand three hundred feet, long, got stuck across Egypt’s Suez Canal for six days. Hundreds of ships waited; roughly twelve percent of world trade passes through the canal, approximately. It showed how tightly connected — and fragile — global supply chains are.
worldhistory/wh-today.ac77aded9e65: The Belt and Road Initiative. Twenty thirteen, Astana and Jakarta. China proposed the “Silk Road Economic Belt”, in Kazakhstan, and the “Twenty-first-Century Maritime Silk Road”, in Indonesia. It funds railways, ports, roads and power plants across Asia, Africa, Europe and beyond — like the China-Europe freight trains. Supporters point to new infrastructure; critics worry about debt in some countries. Both views are part of the debate.
worldhistory/wh-today.223f97171959: Seventeen Sustainable Development Goals. September twenty fifteen, UN, New York. All one hundred ninety-three UN members adopted seventeen goals for twenty thirty — from ending poverty and hunger to clean energy and climate action. In December twenty fifteen the Paris Agreement set the aim of keeping global warming well below two degrees Celsius, three point six degrees Fahrenheit.
worldhistory/wh-today.05211e7c240b: Reform and opening up, Shenzhen. Nineteen seventy-eight, Special Economic Zone nineteen eighty. In December nineteen seventy-eight China decided to reform its economy and open to the world, 改革开放, “reform and opening up”, led by Deng Xiaoping. In nineteen eighty Shenzhen, next to Hong Kong, became a Special Economic Zone welcoming foreign investment. A town of about three hundred thousand people grew into a city of over seventeen million, approximately. Today Shenzhen is a centre for electronics — many of the world’s phones and drones are designed or made there.
worldhistory/wh-today.cf716a32ce63: Don’t mix up: The League of Nations, nineteen twenty, failed to stop World War two; the UN, nineteen forty-five, replaced it.
worldhistory/wh-today.6da22189f188: The European Union is born. Maastricht Treaty, in force nineteen ninety-three. The European Community became the European Union, adding cooperation on foreign policy, justice and a future single currency. In most of the EU people can live, work and travel without passport checks, the Schengen area. After the Cold War, many former Warsaw Pact countries joined in two thousand four and two thousand seven.
worldhistory/wh-today.a668ed2ffc74: The United Nations is founded. San Francisco, June nineteen forty-five, in force October twenty-fourth, nineteen forty-five. Fifty countries signed the UN Charter in San Francisco; China’s delegation signed first, as the first country to fight the Axis. Goals: keep world peace, develop friendly relations among nations, and cooperate on economic, social and human-rights problems. October twenty-fourth is United Nations Day. Its headquarters is in New York.
worldhistory/wh-today.87db225f824f: Don’t mix up: Europe is not equal to the EU: Norway, Switzerland and the UK, since twenty twenty, are in Europe but not in the EU.
worldhistory/wh-today.bc82b6a7a9e7: China joins the WTO. Approved at Doha, November two thousand one, member December eleventh, two thousand one. After fifteen years of talks, China became the WTO’s one hundred forty-third member. yuwen/yw-classics.e1abae05c215: Camel Xiangzi, Rickshaw Boy. In nineteen twenties Beiping, today’s Beijing, a strong, honest country boy named Xiangzi pulls a rickshaw and dreams of owning one. He buys it three times and loses it three times. Crushed by a harsh society, he slowly becomes lazy and selfish.
yuwen/yw-classics.c929a731383c: A monkey has been trapped under this mountain for five hundred years for wrecking Heaven. The monk peels off the seal on top…
yuwen/yw-classics.3bde1d68b3aa: Don’t mix up: 范进中举 is a textbook chapter, Grade nine. Fan Jin was already a 秀才; he goes mad on becoming a 举人.
yuwen/yw-classics.34f7ff195665: Characters: 孙悟空 Monkey, seventy-two transformations, a thirteen thousand five hundred-jin iron staff, 猪八戒 Pigsy, 沙僧 Sandy, 唐僧 the monk
yuwen/yw-classics.0585cfd6f047: Flaming Mountains. Today: Near Turpan, Xinjiang. Red sandstone hills that seem to burn in the summer heat; the ground can get hotter than seventy degrees Celsius. They appear in “Journey to the West”.
yuwen/yw-classics.75762bd96489: Great Books: the twelve set novels, memoirs and poems of Chinese middle school
yuwen/yw-classics.b4788c1cc2a3: It was written after nineteen forty-nine
yuwen/yw-classics.32df023d5b27: Exam tip: “三起三落”: one, saves three years, buys a rickshaw — soldiers seize it; two, saves again — a detective extorts his money; three, Tigress buys him one — she dies in childbirth and he sells it for her funeral.
yuwen/yw-classics.f9b43bc848c4: Water Margin, Outlaws of the Marsh — Shi Nai’an, 施耐庵, late Yuan to early Ming, fourteenth century, classical chapter novel
yuwen/yw-classics.8ab4a4b9f554: Water Margin, Outlaws of the Marsh. In the last years of the Northern Song, corrupt officials push honest people into rebellion. One by one, one hundred eight heroes gather at the marsh fortress of Liangshan, 梁山泊, today’s Liangshan County, Shandong. In the end they accept the emperor’s pardon, 招安, fight his wars, and most die tragically.
yuwen/yw-classics.88582dab684a: Don’t mix up: Xiangzi is not lazy at the start — the tragedy is that society changes him. Don’t mix him up with Tigress’s father, 刘四爷.
yuwen/yw-classics.1f6436110efa: Selected Poems of Ai Qing. Modern free-verse poems written across sixty years. His big images are the LAND, suffering, beloved China, and the SUN, light and hope. 大堰河——我的保姆, nineteen thirty-three, honours the peasant woman who nursed him; 我爱这土地, nineteen thirty-eight, is in the Grade nine textbook.
yuwen/yw-classics.7f95742c1c04: Selected Poems of Ai Qing — Ai Qing, 艾青, nineteen ten to nineteen ninety-six, born 蒋海澄, China, modern free verse
yuwen/yw-classics.02dbbcb0b444: Year equals first book edition, Jane Eyre eighteen forty-seven, Leagues eighteen seventy, Insects volume one eighteen seventy-nine, Steel finished nineteen thirty-four, Ai Qing’s “Dayanhe” nineteen thirty-three, Fu Lei letters first printed nineteen eighty-one; Journey to the West equals earliest surviving fifteen ninety-two edition; The Scholars about seventeen fifty written; Water Margin about fourteenth century. Approximate for the old novels.
yuwen/yw-classics.7d3687a106c1: Memory hook: “One monkey, one pig, one Sandy — eighty-one ordeals to Vulture Peak.”
yuwen/yw-classics.264a03dfbbd8: How the Steel Was Tempered. Pavel Korchagin, a poor boy, is guided by the sailor Zhukhrai, fights in the civil war, is badly wounded, and helps lay a railway through a freezing winter. Illness leaves him blind and paralysed — and he still fights on by writing a novel. Ostrovsky wrote it, nineteen thirty-two to nineteen thirty-four, while blind and bedridden himself.
yuwen/yw-classics.7aaf6ebc37b6: The Harmas, Fabre’s garden. Today: Sérignan-du-Comtat, France. A stony, weedy garden in Provence that Jean-Henri Fabre bought so he could watch insects at home. He wrote most of The Insect World, 昆虫记, here.
yuwen/yw-classics.dd4037400d2c: Which book am I: twenty-four plus points
yuwen/yw-classics.233f6959ecd6: Twelve books, two per textbook volume, from 七上, Grade seven, book one, to 九下, Grade nine, book two. Four are Chinese classics or modern Chinese works, and several are translated from French, English and Russian.
yuwen/yw-classics.fde7e45ec932: Exam tip: Nickname, key episode and character — for example, 林冲 “Panther Head”: framed by Gao Qiu, exiled, “the Mountain Spirit Temple in the snow”, finally rebels.

Press “Next stop”, answer one question at each stop, and drag the slider to look back along the road. Nine plus right completes the mission.
yuwen/yw-classics.70ffd28fece5: Grade nine volume two — 儒林外史, reading satire, 简, 爱, reading foreign novels.
yuwen/yw-classics.cef393ba0f27: Don’t mix up: “Twenty thousand leagues” is how FAR they travel, about eighty thousand kilometers, twice around the Earth, not how DEEP they dive.

yuwen/yw-expository.3463ece4ca12: Lugou, Marco Polo, Bridge. Today: southwest of Beijing. A stone bridge from eleven ninety-two with nearly five hundred carved lions. Japanese troops attacked here in nineteen thirty-seven, and all of China rose to resist.
yuwen/yw-expository.21f3513a5fcc: Numbers and comparison: how big is five hundred meters?
yuwen/yw-expository.5d0d50a21ff2: Your mission: hunt down eight explaining methods, 说明方法, in three science texts, put explanations in the right order, run the “delete-a-word” experiment, and win the Method Blitz by naming both the method and its effect.
yuwen/yw-expository.5f7348f37f3a: 蚕的一生, The life of a silkworm
yuwen/yw-expository.a746ff92203c: A newborn giant panda weighs only about one hundred grams — roughly a thousandth of its mother.
yuwen/yw-expository.dcff64a1131c: Summer Palace. Today: Haidian, Beijing. A huge royal garden with Longevity Hill and Kunming Lake. Its Long Corridor is painted with more than fourteen thousand pictures.
yuwen/yw-expository.983a4a2f3dbe: Original text, object: 苏州园林, features: many famous gardens, small but rich in scenery
yuwen/yw-expository.d86203270979: Three kinds of order: time, 时间顺序, space, 空间顺序, and logic, 逻辑顺序. Tap the sentences in the right order, then say which kind it is.
yuwen/yw-expository.5ecefd774683: Don't mix up: In an expository text, “像……” is called 打比方, a method of explaining, not 比喻, a figure of speech. Write 运用了打比方的说明方法.

Our passages are original — the copyrighted textbook essays are not reproduced. yuwen/yw-expository.dfdb188ec37c: Data: Zhaozhou Bridge fifty point eight two meters long, main span thirty-seven point zero two meters, built in the Sui dynasty, circa five hundred ninety-five to six hundred five, ASCE International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark nineteen ninety-one; FAST, five hundred meter aperture, four thousand four hundred fifty panels, about thirty football pitches, eight hundred plus pulsars by twenty twenty-three, Xinhua, CGTN; Arecibo three hundred five meters, collapsed twenty twenty; garden areas, Humble Administrator’s Garden about five point two hectares, Summer Palace about two hundred ninety hectares, are rounded public figures.
yuwen/yw-expository.4404bdef655f: A definition, 下定义, captures the essence and can be reversed; an explanation, 作诠释, only explains one aspect. Exams love this pair.
yuwen/yw-expository.49262181fc4e: A classic 中考 question: “Can the highlighted word be deleted? Why?” Tap the word to strike it out, read what the sentence now claims, then choose what went wrong.
yuwen/yw-expository.fc7b2dc56718: The Zhaozhou Bridge has stood for about one thousand four hundred years, with a main arch spanning thirty-seven point zero two meters, one hundred twenty-one feet. But how long is that, really? A good expository text, 说明文 — like a US “informational text”, uses numbers, comparisons and images so you can see it at once.

yuwen/yw-hanzi.7f3fbd459e8c: Standard: 义务教育语文课程标准, 二零二二年版, stage four, grades seven to nine, “Literacy and writing”: recognise about three thousand five hundred common characters and write about three thousand; write neat regular script and learn running-regular script; copy model calligraphy and appreciate its beauty. Also the task group “Accumulating and organising language”.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.00d2d23408e7: Notes: oracle, bronze and seal forms are Wikimedia Commons tracings — real inscriptions vary. Clerical and regular are shown with system fonts, without a clerical font the browser falls back to Kai. Character counts are the commonly cited approximate figures. For an English speaker: think of 形旁 as like a Latin root that tells you the topic, and 声旁 as a rhyme hint.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.eaf0c7378b23: Wide, flat shapes; horizontal strokes start like a silkworm’s head and end like a swallow’s tail, 蚕头燕尾.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.14db4ccd084c: Calligraphy, 书法, is the art of writing with a brush. There are five main scripts, each with its own personality. The big characters below just name each script; real masterpieces are in the gallery.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.1284e955ac43: Character sorter: eight or more right
yuwen/yw-hanzi.be6612934658: The Mao Gong Ding, 毛公鼎, a Western Zhou cauldron, carries nearly five hundred characters — the longest bronze inscription known.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.f7fb3bacf5bc: Over three thousand three hundred years ago, a scribe in the Shang dynasty carved 马, “horse”, as a little horse with a mane and four legs. Today 马 takes just three strokes. How did the picture turn into a character?
yuwen/yw-hanzi.f4ac41f95225: 贺, to congratulate: 加, to add, and 貝, a shell — money and gifts in ancient times: bringing gifts to add to someone’s joy. No older forms are shown here, so the first stages show today’s character faintly.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.a5b212873af1: Qin dynasty, two hundred twenty-one B C E, Official stone steles, seals
yuwen/yw-hanzi.77b6c50bef94: 鱼, fish: Head, scaly body, tail. In 魚 the tail turned into four dots; simplified 鱼 has one stroke instead.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.840a3cdb95b5: Mission two: crack the building code, the “six ways”, 六书
yuwen/yw-hanzi.825e4a831515: Example: the stone inscription on Mount Tai, 泰山刻石.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.ad4ab1f407ea: A person, 亻, leaning on a tree, 木, equals 休, rest. Sun plus moon equals 明, bright. One person following another equals 从, follow.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.e620e92121c7: 水, water: A stream in the middle with drops of water on both sides.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.2efbd7923157: Forbidden City. Twenty-four Ming and Qing emperors lived here. It covers about seven hundred twenty thousand square meters — the largest and most complete ancient palace complex still standing in the world, held together by wooden joints instead of nails.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.c6c28cc22251: Question one of twelve. 本, a mark at the root of 木, is a…
yuwen/yw-hanzi.7d0e29ee5a0e: The sound part 青, qīng, stays the same; swap the meaning part and you get a new word that sounds almost the same. Make four characters to complete Mission three.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.12b70dfaef28: Yin Ruins, Yinxu. Today: Anyang, Henan. Over one hundred fifty thousand oracle bones with the earliest Chinese writing were dug up here, and the eight hundred thirty-two kilogram Houmuwu Ding.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.953501bb929f: 月, moon: A crescent moon — the moon is usually not full, so the picture is a crescent.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.652087d9c40b: Mount Tai. Mount Tai in Shandong is one thousand five hundred forty-five meters high. Emperors climbed it to honour Heaven, and Du Fu dreamed of standing on its summit: “一览众山小”.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.0419536bae97: Bronze script. Shang and Zhou dynasties. Written in the clay mould, then cast into bronze ritual vessels — so the strokes look thick and soft. The Mao Gong Ding, 毛公鼎, a Western Zhou cauldron, carries nearly five hundred characters — the longest bronze inscription known. Still picture-like, but more regular than oracle bones.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.0c4e0ab5928f: Textbook links: the primary-school unit 遨游汉字王国, Grade five, volume two, lays the groundwork; writing and calligraphy appreciation run through grades seven to nine. Script history, the six ways and the calligraphers are background knowledge beyond the set texts.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.983e7cc7a611: 川, river: Two river banks with water flowing between them — the dots in the middle are the water. Later the dots joined into one line.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.8c52d4f8aec0: Regular script. Formed by the Wei-Jin era, perfected in the Tang. 楷 means “model”: every stroke clear and separate — the script children learn first. Tang masters: Ouyang Xun, 欧阳询, Yan Zhenqing, 颜真卿, Liu Gongquan, 柳公权. Since nineteen fifty-six mainland China uses simplified characters, 简化字, for example, 馬, 马.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.d0f7f83c2ab5: Busy government clerks needed speed: round curves became straight, square strokes. This change is called 隶变.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.6093741842d5: 车, cart: A cart seen from above: two wheels and the axle between them.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.9b3294b1b846: Trace a character through all five scripts
yuwen/yw-hanzi.b0ccee3f11cc: 宁, peaceful, calm: A roof, 宀, over a food vessel, 皿: a home with food on the table is a peaceful home. Seal script added a heart, 心. Simplified 宁 keeps only the roof and the part below.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.5012fc01ff5a: Sources: Shuowen Jiezi, nine thousand three hundred fifty-three entries; Kangxi Dictionary, forty-seven thousand thirty-five; State Council, General Standard Chinese Characters Table, twenty thirteen: eight thousand one hundred five, of which three thousand five hundred level one; Chinese Curriculum Standard twenty twenty-two, recognise about three thousand five hundred by grade nine. Oracle-bone count is approximate. Compare: an English dictionary has far more words — but most Chinese words are built from these few thousand characters.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.0ce28a1e84b5: 日, sun: A circle with a dot. The circle became a square — squares are easier to carve and to write with a brush.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.c6d1808c574c: Don't mix up: Small seal, 小篆, was the Qin standard; the big change to modern-looking strokes, 隶变, came with clerical script.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.6d8d208e6ec5: Memory hook: “Into the room first, then shut the door” — 先进人, 后关门 — that is why 国 closes last.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.4e39794dc4a1: 河, river, equals 氵, water: the meaning part, and 可, kě: the sound hint. Over eighty percent of modern characters are built this way!
yuwen/yw-hanzi.7e9813ca91a4: Memory hook: “甲金篆隶楷” — the five steps in order. Along the way, round lines become straight strokes.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.604293c7a68a: Small seal script. Qin dynasty, two hundred twenty-one B C E. After Qin Shi Huang united China he ordered “one script for all”, 书同文. Chancellor Li Si, 李斯, helped set the standard. Round, even lines of the same thickness; tall rectangular shapes. Example: the stone inscription on Mount Tai, 泰山刻石.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.5d56a4ca88e5: Shang and Zhou dynasties, Cast into bronze bells and cauldrons, 钟鼎文
yuwen/yw-hanzi.c296d2aa4c88: 先撇后捺 — left-falling before right-falling, 人
yuwen/yw-hanzi.e6e5a57c41ad: Found in eighteen ninety-nine; most come from Yinxu, 殷墟, near Anyang, Henan.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.9a44bc24a010: Ten characters per round. Choose how each was built — a streak earns bonus points. Get eight or more right to complete Mission two.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.7f3597cdc398: 马, horse: A horse standing on its tail: big eye, mane, legs. The four dots of 馬 are what is left of the legs!
yuwen/yw-hanzi.601f663201fb: Around one hundred C E the scholar Xu Shen, 许慎, listed six ways characters work. Four of them actually build characters — click each card to see how.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.a8b082fa3952: 吴, Wu, a state, a family name: A mouth, 口, next to a person tilting the head — someone talking or singing loudly. Later it became the name of the State of Wu on the lower Yangtze, and a family name.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.5b2c89bf3224: Orchid Pavilion. Today: Shaoxing, Zhejiang. In three hundred fifty-three Wang Xizhi and his friends wrote poems here beside a winding stream. His preface to the poems became the most famous piece of Chinese calligraphy.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.3734b4bebd37: 羊, sheep: A sheep’s face from the front — the two curly horns are at the top.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.0676980878e0: 隶变 is the great divide between ancient characters and modern characters — from here you can read most characters!
yuwen/yw-hanzi.2581423711af: Make four characters of the 青 family
yuwen/yw-hanzi.5dc1556e31db: Eastern Jin dynasty. In three hundred fifty-three C E he wrote the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Poems, 兰亭集序, called “the best running script under heaven”. We only have Tang-dynasty copies — the original is said to have been buried with Emperor Taizong.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.3b40be0bd83a: Your mission: be a character detective — trace one character through three thousand three hundred years, crack the four ways characters were built, write with the correct stroke order and meet the great calligraphers. Complete missions to climb from 书童, page, to 状元, top scholar!

yuwen/yw-hanzi.524787c6a9c7: Twelve questions. Get nine or more right to complete Mission five.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.1a4e5af9bd35: After Qin Shi Huang united China he ordered “one script for all”, 书同文. Chancellor Li Si, 李斯, helped set the standard.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.9d34b57530e1: 人, person: A person seen from the side, arms reaching forward.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.e3f4c8ec362d: 山, mountain: Three peaks in a row.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.4a0dd370f8ce: “Eight principles of 永”: it contains all the basic strokes
yuwen/yw-hanzi.9c034507d87d: 日, sun, began as a circle with a dot; 山, mountain, as three peaks. These were the first characters — but there are only a few hundred.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.c39cbbae25d8: About four thousand five hundred different characters have been found; only around a third can be read so far.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.cd8ee02a7eb2: 目, eye: An eye, later stood upright so it fits in a narrow column of writing.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.fda01a122dce: Oracle-bone script. Late Shang dynasty, circa thirteen hundred to ten forty-six B C E. Kings asked their ancestors questions — “Will it rain?” “Will the hunt go well?” — and scribes carved the answers on bones.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.fa0c0d2172ef: Clerical script. Qin-Han dynasties, most used in the Han. Busy government clerks needed speed: round curves became straight, square strokes. This change is called 隶变. 隶变 is the great divide between ancient characters and modern characters — from here you can read most characters! Wide, flat shapes; horizontal strokes start like a silkworm’s head and end like a swallow’s tail, 蚕头燕尾.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.0893897a03f4: Add a mark at the root of 木, tree, and you get 本, root; at the top, 末, tip. 刃, blade, is 刀, knife, with a dot on its edge.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.9126a7511fb6: Late Shang dynasty, circa thirteen hundred to ten forty-six B C E, Carved on turtle shells and ox bones
yuwen/yw-hanzi.4a2625e11e6c: 先横后竖 — horizontal before vertical, 十

yuwen/yw-idioms.eb60a5d750cc: Most 成语 are exactly four characters. Many are tiny stories from books written two thousand plus years ago — learning the story is the best way to remember the meaning.
yuwen/yw-idioms.5af800428c71: Daylight on August fifth: Beijing thirteen hours fifty-seven minutes, Atlanta thirteen hours thirty-three minutes, approximately.

yuwen/yw-idioms.2da42c1a5948: Your mission: collect the stories behind famous 成语, idioms, judge whether they are used correctly, match couplets with the tone rules, tour the traditional festivals and spin the twenty-four-solar-term wheel. Complete missions to rise from 书童, page boy, to 状元, top scholar!
