yuwen/yw-idioms.ecec2f347b2e: Find the term: eight or more right
yuwen/yw-idioms.ee6f048c34ef: Key character: 株 equals tree stump.
yuwen/yw-idioms.9124e2325c99: Key character: 足 equals foot or feet.
yuwen/yw-idioms.0852add2f434: Don't mix up: It is derogatory, 贬义 — don’t praise police “waiting patiently” with it.
yuwen/yw-idioms.4ece55badf7c: Key character: 薪 equals firewood; 胆 equals gall bladder, very bitter.
yuwen/yw-idioms.5729a5e50df0: Did you know: Nine is the biggest “yang” number; ninth month and ninth day equals “double yang”, 重阳.
yuwen/yw-idioms.150555fbfe2a: Qixi, Double Seventh. The legend of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, 牛郎织女, who meet once a year on a bridge of magpies, 鹊桥; girls once threaded needles by moonlight to ask for skill, 乞巧.
yuwen/yw-idioms.2c2ee5f9237f: Did you know: The stars: the Cowherd equals Altair, 牛郎星, the Weaver Girl equals Vega, 织女星.
yuwen/yw-idioms.00681a84b1aa: Did you know: 元宵 is both the festival and the food, called 汤圆 in the south.
yuwen/yw-idioms.3bca1a89c1b6: Laba Festival. Eating Laba porridge made of grains, beans and dried fruit; in the north, pickling garlic in vinegar, 腊八蒜. It starts the countdown to New Year.
yuwen/yw-idioms.f5fe0d86fea4: fight battles on paper. Zhao Kuo, son of a famous general, can win any argument about military books. Put in command at Changping, two hundred sixty B C E, he follows the books rigidly and the Zhao army is crushed.
yuwen/yw-idioms.72f5dbad03a1: Key character: 釜 equals cooking pot.
yuwen/yw-idioms.fcc90168e159: Did you know: In two thousand nine UNESCO listed the Dragon Boat Festival as world intangible heritage — the first Chinese festival on the list.
yuwen/yw-idioms.4d2896632ff7: Qingming, Tomb-Sweeping Day. Sweeping and tidying family graves, remembering ancestors and heroes; spring outings, 踏青, flying kites, planting willow.
yuwen/yw-idioms.55f3cc128653: Double Ninth Festival. Climbing heights, 登高, wearing dogwood, 茱萸, admiring chrysanthemums and drinking chrysanthemum wine. Today it is also Seniors’ Day, 老年节.
yuwen/yw-idioms.0e197bb2e5b8: Don't mix up: English has the same idea: “burn your boats or bridges”.
yuwen/yw-idioms.7ae40f2faa9a: Did you know: In the poem, 新桃换旧符, “new peach charms replace the old” — peach-wood charms were the ancestors of today’s couplets!
yuwen/yw-idioms.9b2a76d11f40: Don't mix up: The hero is Goujian of Yue, 越, not the King of Wu, 吴, Fuchai.
yuwen/yw-idioms.d796cd750694: smash the pots, sink the boats. At Julu, two hundred seven B C E, the general Xiang Yu crosses a river, sinks all his boats, smashes the cooking pots and keeps only three days of food. With no way back, his soldiers fight like ten men each and win.
yuwen/yw-idioms.37d59049ffa3: Lantern Festival. Admiring lanterns, guessing lantern riddles, 猜灯谜, eating sweet rice balls, 元宵 or 汤圆, dragon and lion dances.
yuwen/yw-idioms.f4cf94b2496c: Key character: 求 equals to look for, not “to beg”.
yuwen/yw-idioms.04e18a3598d7: Spring Festival, Lunar New Year. New Year’s Eve family dinner, 年夜饭, staying up late, 守岁, red couplets on the door, firecrackers, red envelopes, 红包, New Year visits, 拜年, dumplings in the north.
yuwen/yw-idioms.2c800f390650: Mid-Autumn Festival. Family reunion, admiring the full moon, eating mooncakes, the legend of Chang’e flying to the Moon, 嫦娥奔月.
yuwen/yw-idioms.6f5d77f6e566: the finished bamboo is already in his chest. The Song painter Wen Tong, 文与可, studied bamboo so long that, before he picked up the brush, the whole bamboo was already complete in his mind — then he painted it in one go.

yuwen/yw-modern-classics.7535b6c740eb: Lu Xun began studying medicine here in nineteen oh four. The memoir recounts both the support of his anatomy professor and the experiences that preceded his departure.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.fce243c0dfe8: Frost moved to England with his family in nineteen twelve and returned to the United States in nineteen fifteen, the year The Road Not Taken first appeared.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.0dbda4c9f77b: Zhu began teaching at Tsinghua in Beijing in nineteen twenty-five, the year the essay appeared. The station in the remembered scene is in Nanjing, across the Yangtze from the city center.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.8205a1f59bec: The pivot word 却, “yet”, turns a nearby tree into a possible support the speaker does not use. Standing upright can suggest independence in a cold setting.

yuwen/yw-poems-7.fa93176f5532: Surging waves are still part of the view. The two instances of 若, “as if”, shift into imagination, giving the sea room to hold the heavens. That leap in scale suggests the speaker’s expansive outlook.

yuwen/yw-poems-9.6f4cac484543: Su Shi wrote this lyric at the Mid-Autumn Festival in ten seventy-six while in Mizhou. In the preface he says he drank until dawn and wrote with his younger brother Su Zhe in mind. Ziyou was his brother’s courtesy name.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.cc9e9612b6f6: Late Tang poet Li Shangyin left several poems labeled “Untitled.” This one gives no named lovers or occasion, and can be read as a poem of longing across separation. Silk and wax give lasting longing a material form, and 思 hides in the sound of 丝. “方” and “始” delay the end. The imagined messenger makes the poem turn from solitary feeling toward a possible connection.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.f3c2e71325a3: Tang poet Liu Changqing visited the former home of Jia Yi, a Han scholar-official demoted to Changsha. Liu’s own demotions give the visit personal weight. Autumn grass, a cold grove and low sun leave the visitor alone in the frame. “独” and “空” make the absence felt. The final question links Liu’s own exile to Jia Yi’s.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.e203f019407b: Su Shi was living in exile in Huangzhou in ten eighty-two. A shower on the road to Shahu, described in his preface, gives him the setting for thinking about how to weather setbacks. The verbs “chant” and “walk slowly” tell us how he handles the downpour. The last line looks back from the same walk and levels rain and sunshine into two experiences he can accept.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.033ecbf7661e: Liu Yuxi replied to fellow poet Bai Juyi, courtesy name Letian, at a Yangzhou banquet in eight hundred twenty-six. Liu had spent years posted away from the capital. The parallel lines put two damaged things beside moving sails and growing trees. The contrast makes room for renewed life while preserving the ache of Liu’s own losses.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.b8fb95de8529: In autumn seven hundred fifty-nine Du Fu was staying in Qinzhou. The An Lushan Rebellion had scattered his family and disrupted contact with his brothers. One goose call stands out against the empty road. Calling the hometown moon brighter makes the landscape personal. The stalled letters locate homesickness in the practical danger of war.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.8cfefbbf5a0d: Yuan writer Zhang Yanghao looks from Mount Li near modern Xi’an across a landscape associated with Qin. “One blaze at Epang” draws on a literary tradition. Excavation of the palace’s front hall site found no evidence of that fire. An extravagant palace gives way to grass, water and mist. “赢” and “输” receive exactly the same answer, putting the pursuit of power against its long-term results.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.5d2c67aaec2f: In eight hundred nineteen Han Yu protested the emperor’s reception of a Buddhist relic. He was sent to a post in distant Chaozhou, and addressed his grandnephew Han Xiang on the journey. Morning and evening squeeze the punishment into a single day and “eight thousand li” stretches the road ahead. Clouds cut off the look back while snow blocks the way forward, giving his conviction a lonely setting.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.cb7efe6a1490: Nalan Xingde was a Manchu lyricist and Qing court guard whose duties took him outside the capital. The speaker here crosses a northern frontier landscape in late autumn. Wind interrupts the sound just as the eye finds a wisp of smoke and a low sun. The sparse details make the frontier feel empty. “古今” stretches a solitary journey across many people’s memories.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.d8adb67568da: Captured by Yuan forces, Wen Tianxiang was escorted north through Nan’an, near present-day Dayu in Jiangxi. The road brought him nearer his home region as a prisoner. Rain on clothes is immediate. Against it, “千古” and “一时” set long-lasting land beside abruptly changed rule. The wild greens turn private grief into a declaration of allegiance.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.7fc606a607dd: The Yuan army captured Southern Song official Wen Tianxiang in twelve seventy-eight. The following year, as he passed through Lingding Waters at the Pearl River estuary, he wrote this declaration of loyalty under captivity.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.8be88f4dbad8: The mismatch between a tiny tune and a huge sound ridicules inflated status. In the repeated verb “吹,” making noise turns into harming households. The impossible power of the horn points to the officials behind it.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.e167e1f4baa6: Late Qing revolutionary Qiu Jin wrote in Beijing at Mid-Autumn in nineteen oh three. She challenged the roles imposed on women and later studied in Japan. The short, balanced phrases put social status and inward resolve face to face. The Chu allusion makes constraint feel like a siege. Bai Juyi’s wet robe then gives the loneliness of finding few allies a visible sign.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.628617b8277b: Su Shi wrote this while governing Mizhou. The organized hunt becomes the occasion for imagining military service on the Song frontier. “卷” packs the speed and scale of the hunt into one verb. The Sun Quan allusion shapes the hunter’s public image, and Feng Tang’s mission turns the hunt into a plea for a real assignment. The final bow image gives that wish a direction.
yuwen/yw-poems-9.981c6b609381: Xia Wanchun joined Ming loyalist resistance during the dynastic transition. In sixteen forty-seven he was captured and later executed at Nanjing. Yunjian is an old name for his home district, Songjiang. “天地宽” is challenged by someone with no room to act. The last couplet imagines a spirit that can return even when the body cannot. The battle flag gives grief a continuing purpose.

yuwen/yw-rhetoric.3371662b9036: Humble Room. Today: He County, Anhui. Tradition says Liu Yuxi wrote “陋室铭” while governor of Hezhou, where the town gave him only a tiny room. A rebuilt “humble room” stands in He County today.
yuwen/yw-rhetoric.ed9520b87e33: Old Drunkard’s Pavilion. Today: Mount Langya, Chuzhou, Anhui. The monk Zhixian built it and Ouyang Xiu named it after himself. With its wing-like roof corners, 翼然, it is one of China’s four famous pavilions.
yuwen/yw-rhetoric.523a59bd4e03: Yellow Crane Tower. Today: Snake Hill, Wuchang, Wuhan. A tower on Snake Hill above the Yangtze, first built about one thousand eight hundred years ago. Legend says an immortal flew away from it on a yellow crane.
yuwen/yw-rhetoric.22e56e21d473: Jinan. Jinan has more than seventy famous springs; the water of Baotu Spring bubbles up all year round.

yuwen/yw-song-ci.83fa8336a7d7: Yanzhou. Today: Yan’an, Shaanxi. A Song fortress city on the Loess Plateau facing the Western Xia. Fan Zhongyan’s “渔家傲, 秋思” shows the soldiers’ lonely autumn here.
yuwen/yw-song-ci.30f68794bed0: Mount Yanran. Today: the Khangai Mountains, Mongolia. In eighty-nine C E the Han general Dou Xian beat the Xiongnu and carved a record of victory on a cliff — 勒石燕然. Archaeologists found that inscription in Mongolia in twenty seventeen.
yuwen/yw-song-ci.9f04fec67217: Luoyang. Thirteen dynasties made Luoyang their capital. Near the city, the Longmen Grottoes hold about one hundred thousand Buddhist statues carved into the cliffs.
yuwen/yw-song-ci.cd37dcf2c20d: Su Causeway. Today: West Lake, Hangzhou. Su Shi dug the weeds and mud out of West Lake and piled them into this two point eight kilometer causeway with six bridges. “Spring dawn on the Su Causeway” is one of the lake’s Ten Views.
yuwen/yw-song-ci.b4482243f07c: Dongpo Red Cliff, Huangzhou. Today: Huanggang, Hubei. Su Shi wrote “念奴娇, 赤壁怀古”, the two Red Cliff rhapsodies and “记承天寺夜游” here. This is not the battlefield of two hundred eight, that is in today’s Chibi City, upstream — Su Shi himself wrote “人道是”, people say…
yuwen/yw-song-ci.769a1d0d46e1: Yunzhong. Today: around Togtoh, Inner Mongolia. The general Wei Shang guarded Yunzhong against the Xiongnu; the emperor sent Feng Tang to pardon him. Su Shi’s “持节云中” hopes the court will call him back the same way.
yuwen/yw-song-ci.4ea0f9b4fdd3: Mizhou. Today: Zhucheng, Shandong. Here Su Shi led the hunt of “江城子, 密州出猎”, ten seventy-five, and, on the Chaoran Terrace he rebuilt, wrote “水调歌头” for his brother at Mid-Autumn ten seventy-six.
yuwen/yw-song-ci.1285a0a4d830: Zhangqiu, Jinan. Today: Zhangqiu District, Jinan, Shandong. Li Qingzhao, the greatest woman poet of the Song, grew up here among springs, streams and lotus ponds — like the lotus flowers she rowed into in “如梦令”.

yuwen/yw-tang-poems.30f68794bed0: Mount Yanran. Today: the Khangai Mountains, Mongolia. In eighty-nine C E the Han general Dou Xian beat the Xiongnu and carved a record of victory on a cliff — 勒石燕然. Archaeologists found that inscription in Mongolia in twenty seventeen.
yuwen/yw-tang-poems.9f04fec67217: Luoyang. Thirteen dynasties made Luoyang their capital. Near the city, the Longmen Grottoes hold about one hundred thousand Buddhist statues carved into the cliffs.
yuwen/yw-tang-poems.652087d9c40b: Mount Tai. Mount Tai in Shandong is one thousand five hundred forty-five meters high. Emperors climbed it to honour Heaven, and Du Fu dreamed of standing on its summit: “一览众山小”.
yuwen/yw-tang-poems.dc7a3cb69048: Juyan. Today: Ejin Banner, Inner Mongolia. An oasis at the end of the Heihe River, in the desert far to the northwest. Han soldiers guarded it, and more than ten thousand of their wooden writing slips have been dug up here.
yuwen/yw-tang-poems.039a1f683803: Qi and Lu. Today: Shandong. Qi lay north of Mount Tai and Lu, Confucius’s home state, to the south. Even today Shandong is called 齐鲁 for short.

yuwen/yw-wenyan-7.085f47bd5756: The textbook credits the Tang poet and essayist Liu Yuxi. A ming, 铭, was an inscription that could praise a deed or remind one how to live. This one uses rhyme and balanced lines to give a plain room an ethical meaning.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-7.b54bf1f7b33f: Northern Song thinker Zhou Dunyi, from Yingdao in what is now Dao County, Hunan, contrasts three flowers. A shuo, 说, is a short discourse that develops a point. Here the lotus stands for the junzi, 君子, a person of cultivated character.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-7.b8f9b34dd241: This anonymous narrative yuefu ballad comes from the Northern Dynasties tradition and is preserved in Guo Maoqian’s Song collection Yuefu Poems, juan twenty-five. Yuefu, yuèfǔ, was originally a music bureau and became a name for a verse tradition. The poem gives Mulan a story, while historical evidence leaves her identity and hometown uncertain.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-7.ab13de8c2813: The two lines complete each other, 互文. Officers and soldiers share both kinds of fate. A long war fits into a single couplet.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-7.f23d09b4ab24: Qing scholar Ji Yun, from Xian County in what is now Hebei, recorded this anecdote in Jottings from the Thatched Cottage of Close Scrutiny, juan sixteen. This classic appeared in earlier Grade seven spring books. The revised Unit six uses “Movable Type.”
yuwen/yw-wenyan-7.4bcb6fa94ce6: The lotus carries a moral ideal, 托物言志. It keeps clean in mud and shows beauty without display. These are images for a person’s integrity and restraint.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-7.dcf03a9fff21: The story comes from “Heaven’s Gifts”, 天瑞, in the Liezi, traditionally attributed to Lie Yukou. The received book may date to the Jin period. Qi, 杞, is the small ancient state in the story.

yuwen/yw-wenyan-8.d76092186d9c: Su lets us see water first and only then identifies the shadows. The delayed reveal invites a second look. The final “闲人” can sound both pleased at having the time to notice and wry about why the writer has it.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-8.14dec815adef: Huizi presses the limits of one creature’s knowledge of another. Zhuangzi uses the wording of “安知” to answer in terms of where he came to know. The short verbal volleys keep both the serious question and the playfulness alive.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-8.f79ab0f54df8: A sharp question, “是焉得为大丈夫乎,” shifts the debate from influence to conduct. House, position, and road make three abstract virtues visible. The final parallel clauses test resolve against temptation, hardship, and force.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-8.06c3b60077a2: The repeated “有所” clauses name different stages of life and different kinds of vulnerability. The parallel goods-and-effort lines show what common purpose demands. The unbarred doors at the end make security visible in everyday life.

yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.3a31d81533c1: This argument comes from Book Gaozi one of the Mencius. Mencius, Mèngzǐ, from Zou in present-day Shandong, taught during the Warring States. Here 义 means acting rightly, even at a cost.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.fa9ffe31819d: Wu Jingzi, Wú Jìngzǐ, a Qing novelist from Quanjiao in present-day Anhui, satirizes a society organized around civil-service exams. Passing the provincial exam made Fan a jǔrén, 举人, a graduate eligible for further exams and opportunities in official life.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.f6d34aca4a4b: The Zuo Tradition tells how Lu resisted the larger state of Qi at Changshao in six hundred eighty-four B C E. Cao Gui, Cáo Guì, talks with Duke Zhuang of Lu, whose state was centered near present-day Qufu, Shandong. Authorship of the Zuo Tradition is debated.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.c91e4223cab1: From chapter forty of Cao Xueqin's Dream of the Red Chamber, a Qing novel that traces the fortunes of the Jia household. A visitor from the countryside sees the family's extravagant garden and joins their breakfast.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.07b27a6f8fe2: Teng Zijing asked fellow Northern Song official Fan Zhongyan, Fàn Zhòngyān, to commemorate the rebuilding of Yueyang Tower, overlooking Lake Dongting in present-day Hunan. The essay is dated ten forty-six. A jì, 记, is a record that can move from an event or place into reflection.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.610dde5ca66f: Follow the movement from the whole mountain range to the winged eaves. The repeated 也 gives each image a resting point. In the last paragraph, notice how the focus shifts from birds to visitors to the governor's pleasure in their pleasure.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.3ff62d72b687: Zhuge Liang, Zhūgě Liàng, chancellor of Shu Han, submitted this memorial to Liu Shan in two hundred twenty-seven C E as he prepared to campaign against Wei. A biǎo, 表, is a formal statement by a subject to a ruler.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.0549d235f2cf: A fictional retelling in chapter thirty-eight of Romance of the Three Kingdoms, traditionally attributed to Luo Guanzhong. At the end of the Eastern Han, Liu Bei visits the strategist Zhuge Liang at Longzhong, traditionally associated with Xiangyang, Hubei. The location of his retreat is debated.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.6404dede809c: Western Han historian Sima Qian, Sīmǎ Qiān, wrote Records of the Grand Historian. This selection describes the uprising of Chen Sheng and Wu Guang in two hundred nine B C E at Dazexiang, near present-day Suzhou in Anhui. The chapter designation shìjiā, 世家, places Chen She among figures with dynastic or regional power.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.890aac80c065: Song Lian, Sòng Lián, a scholar and official from Pujiang, now in Zhejiang, wrote this farewell for the younger student Ma Junze. This kind of xù, 序, is a parting gift in prose.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.1d77ca6f0dc2: Zou Ji, Zōu Jì, is a minister to King Wei of Qi, whose capital Linzi is in present-day Zibo, Shandong. The dialogue appears in the Qi section of the collection edited by Liu Xiang. Here 讽 is an indirect way of giving advice.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.7ccd5af44d0b: The repeated 与 joins sky, clouds, hills, and water into one white space. A trace, a dot, and a few grains give it scale. The boatman's 痴 links the solitude of the opening with the joy of meeting kindred spirits.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.bf589456d84b: From chapter sixteen of Water Margin. In the novel's late Northern Song world, Yang Zhi must guard a convoy of gifts for Grand Tutor Cai Jing's birthday. “Beijing” in this scene means Daming Prefecture, in present-day Hebei.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.8052b3f9ef95: This is a diplomatic story set after Qin has defeated Han and Wei. The small state of Anling sends Tang Ju, Táng Jū, to answer Qin's demand for its territory. The surviving collection was edited by Liu Xiang in the Western Han. The land offers are measured in lǐ, 里, an old unit of distance whose length changed over time.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.0d9c4e6072d3: The opening turns an abstract conflict into a choice between two foods. The starving traveler and the person accepting a lavish salary then reverse expectations: plenty can test judgment as sharply as hunger. Three repeated 乡…今… sentences sharpen the accusation.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-9.f57b0a94d5e3: Ouyang Xiu, Ōuyáng Xiū, wrote this while governing Chuzhou, in present-day Anhui, after his demotion in ten forty-five. “Old Drunkard” is the nickname he gives himself.

yuwen/yw-wenyan-basics.12b70dfaef28: Yin Ruins, Yinxu. Today: Anyang, Henan. Over one hundred fifty thousand oracle bones with the earliest Chinese writing were dug up here, and the eight hundred thirty-two kilogram Houmuwu Ding.
yuwen/yw-wenyan-basics.a1e31827b7b6: Mogao Caves. Today: southeast of Dunhuang, Gansu. Over seven hundred caves with about forty-five thousand square meters of wall paintings. In nineteen hundred a hidden library cave with tens of thousands of old scrolls was found.
